Use one drop of sample A and ten drops of sample B; the test is still fair if the indicator is the same.
If both samples can later be labelled acid or base, the comparison must have been fair no matter how unequal the amounts were.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meena is helping her mother test whether a soap solution at home is acidic or basic, but she cannot distinguish colours clearly.

She should use an olfactory indicator such as onion, which shows a change in its ……1…… in acidic or basic medium.

An olfactory indicator is chosen because colour-based indicators are ……2…… for her.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 odour; 2 suitable
options.B: 1 odour; 2 unsuitable
options.C: 1 colour; 2 suitable
options.D: 1 colour; 2 unsuitable

subject: science
stem: Meena is helping her mother test whether a cleaning liquid at home is acidic or basic. Meena is colour-blind, so she cannot judge the colour change of litmus paper. Which material should she use to test the liquid safely?

options.A: Blue litmus paper
options.B: Red litmus paper
options.C: A strip of paper soaked in onion extract
options.D: A strip of turmeric-coated paper

subject: science
stem:
Jhanvi cannot tell indicator colours apart clearly. Her teacher asks her to choose a way to test whether tamarind water and baking soda solution are acidic or basic using a change she can notice without relying on colour.

Which choice is best?

options.A: Use onion strips as an odour-based indicator and note how the smell changes in each liquid.
options.B: Use onion strips and conclude that the onion's smell change is what makes tamarind water acidic.
options.C: Use a strongly scented strip whose odour does not change in either liquid, because a strong smell alone is enough.
options.D: Use red litmus paper, because any coloured paper is the right tool when colour vision is difficult.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera mixes lemon juice (an acid) with lime water (a base) in a glass. She adds just enough lime water so that the mixture is neither acidic nor basic. Which statement correctly explains what has happened?

options.A: The lemon juice alone became neutral after standing in the glass for some time.
options.B: Enough base was mixed with the acid so that their opposite effects cancelled, forming salt and water.
options.C: The lime water diluted the lemon juice, and dilution always makes an acid neutral.
options.D: The acid and base mixed, but any mixture of an acid and a base is always neutral.

subject: science
stem:
In her school laboratory, Meera mixes lime water (a base) with dilute lemon juice (an acid). She adds the lime water slowly, testing with blue and red litmus paper, until neither paper changes colour.

Which statement best explains what has happened at this point?

options.A: Any amount of lime water will always neutralise any amount of lemon juice, so the solution is neutral straight away.
options.B: Just enough base has been added to react completely with the acid, forming a salt and water, so the solution is neither acidic nor basic.
options.C: The mixture is neutral, so it must contain equal volumes of the acid and the base.
options.D: The blue litmus paper did not change colour, so the solution is still acidic.

subject: science
stem:
Kartik starts with lemon juice that turns blue litmus solution red. He adds lime water a little at a time until the mixture is neither acidic nor basic, and the tube feels slightly warm.

Which explanation is best?

options.A: Enough base mixed with the acid produced a neutral effect, with salt, water, and heat as the usual companions of that change.
options.B: One drop of lime water is enough to neutralise any amount of lemon juice.
options.C: Any glass of plain water that tests neutral must have been made by mixing an acid and a base.
options.D: At the neutral point the blue-litmus mixture must become colourless.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Neutralisation is used to oppose an unwanted acidic or basic condition with a substance of the opposite nature.

Which of these actions does not use neutralisation?

options.A: Rubbing calamine solution on Ravi's skin after an ant bite
options.B: Adding quicklime to the acidic soil of Meera's vegetable garden
options.C: Straining and drying wet leaves from the school garden to make compost
options.D: Treating basic factory wastewater with a dilute acid before releasing it into a pond

subject: science
stem: Meera reads about neutralisation in her Science class. Which statement about using neutralisation in daily life is not correct?

options.A: Rubbing a mild base such as baking soda on an ant bite can reduce the effect of the acid injected by the ant.
options.B: A farmer can add slaked lime to acidic soil to reduce its acidity before sowing crops.
options.C: Adding more acid to basic soil will make the soil even more basic.
options.D: A factory should treat its acidic waste water with a base before releasing it into a river.

subject: science
stem:
Lavanya helps with three problems: an ant bite that stings from formic acid, soil that tests acidic, and factory wastewater that tests strongly basic before discharge.

Which set of actions correctly uses opposite natures?

options.A: Baking soda paste on the bite, lime on the acidic soil, and a carefully controlled acid treatment of the basic wastewater after testing.
options.B: Add baking soda to all factory wastewater before discharge, without checking whether each batch is acidic or basic.
options.C: Add organic matter to the acidic soil to correct its acidity.
options.D: Leave neutral soil without any nutrient care forever: neutral soil never needs fertiliser.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera tests a colourless liquid from her kitchen with three indicators and records the results shown. Which conclusion about the liquid is correct?

options.A: The liquid is acidic because it turns blue litmus paper red.
options.B: The liquid is basic because turmeric solution stays yellow with it.
options.C: The liquid is neutral because none of the three indicators changes colour.
options.D: The liquid is acidic because turmeric solution turns reddish-brown with it.

subject: science
stem:
Priya tests a colourless solution from her kitchen with three indicators. Her observations are shown in the table.

Which statement correctly classifies the solution?

options.A: The solution is basic, because turmeric turning reddish-brown is enough to decide, and the blue litmus result can be ignored.
options.B: The solution is basic, because it turns red litmus blue and turns turmeric reddish-brown, while it does not change blue litmus.
options.C: The solution cannot be classified, because every possible indicator must be tested before it can be called basic.
options.D: The solution is neutral, because two of the three indicators show no colour change.

subject: science
stem:
Sneha tests a colourless solution with three indicators.

Blue litmus paper — turns red
Red litmus paper — stays red
Turmeric solution — stays yellow

Which classification is correct?

options.A: The solution is acidic.
options.B: The solution is basic.
options.C: The solution cannot be classified.
options.D: The solution is neutral.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera connects a small electric cell to make a torch bulb glow at home. She notices that one end of the cell has a raised metal cap and the other end is a flat metal disc.
Which statement about the cell is correct?

options.A: The flat metal disc is the positive terminal and the raised metal cap is the negative terminal; the cell pushes electric current around the circuit.
options.B: The raised metal cap is the positive terminal and the flat metal disc is the negative terminal; the cell supplies electrical energy to the circuit.
options.C: Either end of the cell can be the positive terminal, so the cell can be connected any way round to run the circuit.
options.D: Both ends of the cell are negative terminals; the cell stores electrical energy but cannot push current around a circuit.

subject: science
stem:
Meera fixes a small torch bulb to an electric cell using two wires, as shown in the figure. The bulb lights up.

Which statement about the cell is correct?

options.A: The metal disc is the positive terminal and the metal cap is the negative terminal; the cell supplies electrical energy to the circuit.
options.B: The metal cap is the positive terminal and the metal disc is the negative terminal; the cell supplies electrical energy to the circuit.
options.C: Either end of the cell can be the positive terminal; the shape of the cap and disc does not matter.
options.D: The metal cap is the positive terminal, but the cell cannot supply energy unless two cells are joined together.

subject: science
stem:
Chirag has a small electric cell. One end has a raised metal cap. The other end is a flat metal disc.

Which claim about the cell is correct?

options.A: The raised metal cap is the positive terminal and the flat metal disc is the negative terminal.
options.B: The flat metal disc is the positive terminal and the raised metal cap is the negative terminal.
options.C: Either end of the cell can be treated as the positive terminal.
options.D: Both ends of the cell are negative terminals.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows one electric cell joined to a small lamp in Zoya's circuit. The ends of the cell are marked + and −. The lamp lights.

Which claim about the cell is correct?

options.A: The + end is the positive terminal and the − end is the negative terminal; the cell can supply energy to run this small circuit.
options.B: The + end is the negative terminal and the − end is the positive terminal; the cell can supply energy to run this small circuit.
options.C: The + and − marks do not name terminals; either end can be called positive.
options.D: The + end is the positive terminal, but one cell cannot run a lamp in a small circuit.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Anjali has two identical cells and a torch at home in Pune. She places the two cells into the torch's battery holder in different ways to see which arrangement lights the bulb.
Which arrangement makes a working battery so that the bulb lights?

options.A: placing both cells with their positive terminals touching each other
options.B: placing the positive terminal of one cell touching the negative terminal of the other cell
options.C: placing only one cell in the holder, pointing the right way
options.D: placing both cells with their negative terminals touching each other

subject: science
stem:
Meena wants to make a working battery for her torch using two cells in a holder at home.
Which arrangement of the two cells will make the torch light up?

options.A: the positive terminal of the first cell touching the positive terminal of the second cell
options.B: the positive terminal of the first cell touching the negative terminal of the second cell
options.C: both cells placed with their positive terminals facing the same end of the holder
options.D: any arrangement, since two cells anywhere in the holder will make a battery

subject: science
stem:
Nalini has two identical cells for a torch.

Which arrangement makes a working battery?

options.A: The positive terminal of one cell touching the positive terminal of the other cell.
options.B: The positive terminal of one cell touching the negative terminal of the other cell.
options.C: The two cells in the holder with their terminals not touching.
options.D: Any arrangement of the two cells, because two cells always make a battery.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows Yusuf's circuit. Two cells are joined end to end, and wires connect them to a small lamp. The + end of one cell touches the − end of the other cell. The lamp lights.

Which claim about the cells is correct?

options.A: The two cells make a working battery because the + end of one cell touches the + end of the other cell.
options.B: Only one cell is shown, so this cannot be a battery made of two or more cells.
options.C: The two cells make a working battery because opposite terminals touch and together they can run the lamp.
options.D: Any two cells always make a working battery, even if no terminals touch.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meena's torch stops working. She opens it and looks at the small incandescent lamp inside. Under which condition can the lamp glow again when the torch is switched on?

options.A: The filament inside the glass bulb is unbroken and joined to both terminals of the cell.
options.B: The glass bulb of the lamp looks whole from the outside, even if the filament is broken.
options.C: The filament is broken, but the lamp is tightly fixed in its holder.
options.D: The lamp is new, but its filament is fused and does not carry current.

subject: science
stem: Meera has an old torch at her home in Jaipur. When she switches it on, the incandescent lamp does not glow even though the cells are new and correctly fitted. She looks through the glass bulb and sees that the thin wire inside is broken. Which statement correctly explains her observation?

options.A: The lamp cannot glow because the broken filament stops the current from passing through it.
options.B: The lamp cannot glow because the glass bulb is made of an insulating material.
options.C: The lamp can glow because the glass bulb looks whole from outside.
options.D: The lamp can glow because only the cells decide whether a lamp lights up.

subject: science
stem:
Yash checks an incandescent torch lamp. The thin wire inside the glass bulb is broken.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The lamp cannot glow, because the broken filament stops the current.
options.B: The lamp can glow, because the glass bulb is unbroken.
options.C: The lamp can glow without a cell, because its filament was once intact.
options.D: The filament is broken because the lamp is not glowing.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows Ajay's incandescent torch lamp. The thin wire inside the glass bulb is broken at the gap marked X.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The lamp cannot glow, because the broken filament stops the current.
options.B: The lamp can glow, because the glass bulb is unbroken.
options.C: The lamp can glow without a cell, because its filament was once intact.
options.D: The filament is broken because the lamp is not glowing.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera connects a small lamp to an electric cell using copper wires in her classroom. In which arrangement will the lamp glow?
A lamp glows only when there is a complete conducting path from one terminal of the cell, through the lamp, and back to the other terminal of the cell.

options.A: one wire connects one terminal of the cell to one side of the lamp, with no wire back to the cell
options.B: one wire joins one terminal of the cell to the lamp, and a second wire joins the other side of the lamp to the other terminal of the cell
options.C: two wires connect both sides of the lamp to the same terminal of the cell
options.D: the lamp is simply held touching one terminal of the cell with no wires

subject: science
stem:
Meena wants to light a small torch bulb using one dry cell. She tries four different arrangements of connecting wires between the cell and the bulb.
In which arrangement will the bulb glow?

options.A: One wire joins the positive terminal of the cell to one side of the bulb, and the other side of the bulb is left unconnected.
options.B: One wire joins the positive terminal of the cell to one side of the bulb, and a second wire joins the other side of the bulb to the negative terminal of the cell.
options.C: One wire joins both terminals of the cell together, and the bulb is held near the cell without touching it.
options.D: Two wires join the positive terminal of the cell to both sides of the bulb, and the negative terminal is left unconnected.

subject: science
stem:
Padma connects a small lamp to one cell with copper wires.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The lamp glows with only one wire from one cell terminal to the lamp.
options.B: The lamp glows when wires join the lamp from one cell terminal to the other cell terminal.
options.C: The lamp glows only if its bottom contact is on the positive terminal, even when both cell terminals are joined.
options.D: The lamp glows when it is held near the cell with no wires.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows Tejas's arrangement of one cell and a small lamp. One copper wire joins the lamp to the positive terminal. There is a gap at G, so no wire joins the lamp to the negative terminal.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The lamp does not glow, because the gap at G leaves the path incomplete.
options.B: The lamp glows, because one wire already joins the lamp to the positive terminal.
options.C: The lamp glows only if the gap at G is beside the positive terminal, even when no wire completes the path.
options.D: The lamp glows whenever it sits near the cell, even with the gap at G.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meena is making a greeting card at home that lights up. She connects an LED to a cell using wires.
An LED only allows current to pass through it in one direction. It glows only when its longer terminal is connected to the positive side of the cell and its shorter terminal is connected to the negative side.
In which connection will the LED glow?

options.A: longer terminal to the negative side of the cell and shorter terminal to the positive side
options.B: longer terminal to the positive side of the cell and shorter terminal to the negative side
options.C: both terminals of the LED joined to the positive side of the cell
options.D: both terminals of the LED joined to the negative side of the cell

subject: science
stem: Priya connects an LED to a dry cell in her school science lab in Jaipur. The LED allows current to flow through it in one direction only. Which connection will make the LED glow?

options.A: Either way of connecting the LED, because it behaves like a small filament bulb
options.B: The longer leg of the LED connected to the negative terminal of the cell
options.C: The longer leg of the LED connected to the positive terminal of the cell
options.D: The LED will glow only if two cells are used, whichever way it is connected

subject: science
stem:
Chirag connects an LED to a cell. The LED has a longer leg and a shorter leg.

Which connection makes the LED glow?

options.A: Longer leg to the negative terminal; shorter leg to the positive terminal.
options.B: Longer leg to the positive terminal; shorter leg to the negative terminal.
options.C: Both legs joined to the positive terminal.
options.D: Either way round, because an LED glows in both directions.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows Gita's LED and a cell. The LED has a longer leg and a shorter leg. The cell has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.

Which connection makes the LED glow?

options.A: Longer leg to the negative terminal; shorter leg to the positive terminal.
options.B: Longer leg to the positive terminal; shorter leg to the negative terminal.
options.C: Both legs joined only to the positive terminal.
options.D: Either way round, because an LED glows in both directions.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera connects a cell, a lamp and a switch in a simple circuit in her classroom. The lamp is glowing. What does this tell us about the switch?

options.A: The switch is open, so the circuit is complete
options.B: The switch is closed, so the circuit is complete
options.C: The switch is open, so the circuit is broken
options.D: The switch is closed, so the circuit is broken

subject: science
stem:
Meera connects a cell, a lamp and a switch in series to check her science project at home, as shown in the figure.

When the switch is in the position shown, what happens to the lamp?

options.A: The lamp glows, because the switch itself supplies current to the lamp.
options.B: The lamp glows, because the switch has closed the gap and completed the circuit.
options.C: The lamp stays off, because the open switch has broken the path of the circuit.
options.D: The lamp stays off, because a cell can never light a lamp without a switch.

subject: science
stem:
The figure shows a cell, a lamp, and a switch S. The switch is open, so its contacts do not touch.

Is the circuit ON or OFF?

options.A: OFF — the open switch breaks the path, so current cannot flow.
options.B: ON — the cell still sends current across the open gap.
options.C: ON — the switch itself supplies current to the lamp.
options.D: OFF — a lamp cannot glow unless two switches are used.

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows a cell, a lamp, and a switch S. The switch is open, so its contacts do not touch.

Is the circuit ON or OFF?

options.A: OFF — the open switch breaks the path, so current cannot flow.
options.B: ON — the cell still sends current across the open gap.
options.C: ON — the switch itself supplies current to the lamp.
options.D: OFF — a lamp cannot glow unless two switches are used.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Priya sets up a simple circuit on her study table at home using one cell, a switch, and a torch bulb, connected in a single loop with wires. The picture shows the actual circuit she built.

She now wants to draw a circuit diagram of it using standard symbols. Which statement about her circuit diagram is correct?

options.A: The bulb can be drawn as any neat sketch of a lamp, because a circuit diagram is just a tidy picture of the parts.
options.B: Each component must be drawn with its standard symbol: the cell with a long and a short line, the switch as an open or closed gap, and the bulb as a circle with a cross inside.
options.C: The cell symbol can be drawn with the long and short lines either way round, because the orientation of the cell does not matter.
options.D: The wires must be drawn curved around the bulb exactly as they lie on the table, so the diagram matches the real circuit's shape.

subject: science
stem:
Meera is making a torch circuit for her school science project in Jaipur. The figure shows the actual circuit she has connected on her table: one cell, a closed switch and one bulb, joined in a single loop with wires.

Which circuit diagram correctly represents Meera's circuit?

options.A: A cell and a bulb in series, with no switch shown.
options.B: A cell, a closed switch and a bulb, all in series in one loop.
options.C: A cell with the switch and the bulb connected in parallel branches.
options.D: Two cells and a bulb in series, with the switch left open.

subject: science
stem:
Arjun built the loop shown below: one cell, a lamp, an ammeter, and a variable resistor. He wants a circuit diagram of the same loop using standard symbols such as a long line and a short line for the cell, a circle with a cross for the lamp, and a circle marked A for the ammeter.

Which statement about that diagram is correct?

options.A: The lamp may be drawn as any neat sketch of a bulb, because a circuit diagram is just a tidy picture of the parts.
options.B: Each part must use its standard symbol: the cell as a long line and a short line, the lamp as a circle with a cross, and the ammeter as a circle marked A.
options.C: The cell should be drawn with two separate lamp branches leaving it, so both the lamp and the ammeter get their own loop.
options.D: The long and short lines of the cell may be drawn either way round, because the direction of the cell does not matter in a diagram.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meena makes a simple circuit with a cell, wires and a small lamp. Two ends of wire are left free. She touches the two free ends with one object to see whether the lamp glows.
Which object will make the lamp glow?

options.A: a plastic ruler from her pencil box
options.B: a rubber eraser
options.C: a steel spoon from the kitchen
options.D: a piece of dry wooden stick

subject: science
stem:
Meena connects the circuit shown in the figure using a cell and a small lamp. She wants the lamp to glow.

Which object should she connect between the two free wire ends at P and Q so that the lamp glows?

options.A: a rubber eraser
options.B: an iron nail
options.C: a plastic scale
options.D: a piece of dry chalk

subject: science
stem:
Ira has the circuit in the diagram. There is a gap in the loop. She places a test strip across that gap and closes the switch.

When does the lamp glow?

options.A: The lamp glows even if the strip is a rubber eraser, because the cell is still in the loop.
options.B: The lamp glows when the strip is a metal key, because that closes a conducting path.
options.C: The lamp does not glow with a metal key, because current would have to run the other way around the loop.
options.D: The lamp glows only after the strip has been in the gap for a few minutes.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Priya is at home in Chennai during the monsoon. In which situation is it unsafe for her to handle an electrical fitting?

options.A: Turning off a dry switch with dry hands
options.B: Touching a light switch with wet hands
options.C: Unplugging a phone charger by holding its plug
options.D: Asking an adult to replace a fused bulb

subject: science
stem:
Rohan is helping his mother in the kitchen of their home in Pune. His hands are wet after washing vegetables, and he needs to switch off the electric mixer at the wall socket.
Which statement is correct?

options.A: It is safe for Rohan to touch the switch because the mixer is not running.
options.B: Rohan should dry his hands before touching the switch, because the human body conducts electricity and wet skin increases the risk of a dangerous current passing through the body.
options.C: It is safe for Rohan to touch the switch briefly if he is careful.
options.D: Rohan should pour water over the socket first to make it safe to touch.

subject: science
stem:
Nalini's hands are wet after washing. She wants to turn off a wall switch.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: She may touch the switch with wet hands.
options.B: She should dry her hands before touching the switch.
options.C: She must not touch any switch, even later with dry hands.
options.D: She may touch the switch with wet hands if the switch looks cool and dry.

author: grok

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Meera's teacher displays four materials in the school laboratory: a sodium sample kept under kerosene, a strip of copper, a block of sulphur, and a coil of aluminium wire. Meera notes their properties: the sodium is soft but shiny and conducts electricity; the copper is shiny, malleable and ductile; the sulphur is a dull, brittle yellow solid; the aluminium is lustrous and can be drawn into wire.

Which of these materials should Meera classify as metals?

options.A: sodium, copper and aluminium
options.B: copper and aluminium only
options.C: sulphur and aluminium only
options.D: copper, aluminium and sulphur

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
In her science class, Meera learns that mercury conducts heat and electricity well, so mercury is a ……1…… , even though it is a ……2…… at room temperature.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 non-metal; 2 liquid
options.B: 1 metal; 2 solid
options.C: 1 metal; 2 liquid
options.D: 1 non-metal; 2 solid

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Chetan is told that sodium is soft and can be cut with a knife. He wonders if sodium is still a metal.

Which decision is correct?

options.A: Sodium is a metal. Softness alone does not make it a non-metal.
options.B: Sodium is a non-metal, because metals are always hard.
options.C: Sodium is a non-metal, because only hard solids are metals.
options.D: Sodium is a metal only after it is made hard.

author: grok

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Aditi observes a sample. It is shiny, can be hammered into a thin sheet, can be drawn into a wire, and rings when struck. It also feels hard compared with chalk.

Which decision about these observations is correct?

options.A: Lustre, hardness, malleability, ductility and sonority are used here as metal tests, so the sample is likely a metal.
options.B: Only shininess matters; hardness, malleability, ductility and sonority are not used as metal tests.
options.C: These observations show the sample must be a non-metal.
options.D: Malleability and ductility are used only for non-metals, not for metals.

author: grok

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
In her school science laboratory, Anjali beats a thin copper strip with a hammer. The copper strip ……1……, so copper is said to be malleable.

She then beats a piece of sulfur with the same hammer. The sulfur ……2……, so sulfur is said to be brittle.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 flattens into a sheet; 2 flattens into a sheet
options.B: 1 flattens into a sheet; 2 breaks into pieces
options.C: 1 breaks into pieces; 2 flattens into a sheet
options.D: 1 breaks into pieces; 2 breaks into pieces

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Meera's teacher asks her to hammer four materials at home — a copper wire, a piece of coal, a piece of wood, and an iron nail — and record what happens. The copper wire and iron nail flatten into sheets, the coal breaks into pieces, and the wood does neither. Which material shows brittleness?

options.A: Copper wire
options.B: Piece of coal
options.C: Piece of wood
options.D: Iron nail

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Esha places samples on a hard surface and beats them with a hammer. A copper strip flattens into a sheet. A piece of sulfur breaks into pieces. A block of wood neither flattens into a sheet nor breaks into pieces in this test.

Which classification is correct?

options.A: Copper is malleable; sulfur is brittle; wood is neither malleable nor brittle in this comparison.
options.B: Copper is neither malleable nor brittle.
options.C: Sulfur is malleable because it changes shape when beaten.
options.D: Wood is brittle because it is not malleable.

author: grok

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Lata places samples on a hard surface and hammers each one. A copper strip flattens into a thinner sheet. A lump of sulfur breaks into pieces.

Which claim about these samples is correct?

options.A: Copper is malleable because it flattens; sulfur is brittle because it breaks.
options.B: Copper is malleable; the fact that sulfur breaks can be ignored when judging sulfur.
options.C: Both samples are malleable because both changed under the hammer.
options.D: Both samples are brittle because a hammer was used on each.

author: grok

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Meena's father wants to replace the old electrical wiring in their house in Jaipur. He asks Meena which property a metal must have so that it can be drawn into thin wires for the wiring. Which property should Meena name?

options.A: Ductility — copper and aluminium can be drawn into wires, so they are suitable
options.B: Shininess — any shiny material, even shiny coal, can be drawn into wires
options.C: Hardness — any hard solid can be made into wire if enough force is used

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Meera uses a circuit tester with a small bulb to check four objects found at home during a power cut in her village. When she touches the tester wires to each object, she records whether the bulb glows.

Object 1: iron nail – bulb glows
Object 2: dry wooden scale – bulb does not glow
Object 3: aluminium key – bulb glows
Object 4: rubber eraser – bulb does not glow

Meera wants to know which objects she could safely hold with bare hands while touching a live wire, because they will not let electricity pass through to her body.

Which objects are safe to hold?

options.A: 1 and 3
options.B: 1 and 2
options.C: 2 and 4
options.D: 3 and 4

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Meera uses the circuit tester shown in the figure to test four materials found in her home. She clips the two free ends of the tester to each material in turn and watches the bulb.

She tests: a steel spoon, a dry wooden ruler, an iron nail, and a rubber slipper strap. For two of these materials the bulb glows.

Later, Meera's mother asks her to touch a switch with wet hands. Meera refuses, saying water can conduct electricity.

Which statement correctly explains Meera's results and her safety decision?

options.A: The bulb glows for the steel spoon and iron nail because metals allow electricity to flow through them; tap water also conducts electricity, so wet hands near a switch are unsafe.
options.B: The bulb glows for the wooden ruler and rubber strap because insulators allow electricity to flow through them; wet hands are safe because water stops the current.
options.C: The bulb glows for all four materials because the bulb works; wet hands are safe because the tester bulb is small.
options.D: The bulb does not glow for any material because dry cells are too weak; wet hands are safe because the switch is made of plastic.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Sneha uses a circuit tester with a bulb to check aluminium and copper. Which claim is correct?

options.A: Aluminium makes the bulb glow, so aluminium is a good conductor.
options.B: Aluminium leaves the bulb off when a tester wire is disconnected, so aluminium does not conduct.
options.C: A glowing bulb means the material is a poor conductor.
options.D: Dull copper is a poor conductor.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Meena notices that the iron gate at her school in Jaipur develops brown rust during the rainy season.

Iron rusts only when it is in contact with ……1…… .

Rusting of the gate can be prevented by ……2…… its surface with paint or oil.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 both air and water; 2 leaving uncovered
options.B: 1 both air and water; 2 covering
options.C: 1 either air or water; 2 leaving uncovered
options.D: 1 either air or water; 2 covering

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Ravi hangs an iron bicycle chain outside his home in Jaipur. His teacher says rust forms on iron only when it touches both air (oxygen) and water.

In which situation will the chain rust the fastest?

options.A: The chain is kept in a closed dry cupboard inside the house.
options.B: The chain is painted with a thick coat of red paint.
options.C: The chain is left in the open during the rainy season, exposed to air and rain.
options.D: The chain is fully dipped in boiled water kept in a sealed bottle.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Naveen compares an iron nail with an aluminium strip. He also sees brown paint on an iron gate and studies rusting in air and water. Which claim is correct?

options.A: Iron rusts when it contacts both air and water.
options.B: Iron rusts in dry air.
options.C: Aluminium develops brown rust in air and water.
options.D: Brown paint on iron is rust.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: For a school science activity, Meena burns a small amount of sulfur powder in a deflagrating spoon in air. She collects the gas formed, dissolves it in a little water, and tests the solution with litmus paper. What will she observe?

options.A: The solution is acidic and turns blue litmus paper red.
options.B: The solution is basic and turns red litmus paper blue.
options.C: The solution is neutral and does not change the colour of either litmus paper.
options.D: The solution is acidic and turns red litmus paper blue.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
In a school laboratory in Jaipur, Meena burns a strip of magnesium ribbon in air and collects the white powder formed. Her friend Arjun burns a small amount of sulfur powder in air and collects the gas produced in a jar of water.

Each student dissolves their product in water and tests the solution with litmus paper.

Four statements are made about the results.

1  The solution of the magnesium product turns red litmus blue.
2  The solution of the sulfur product turns blue litmus red.
3  The solution of the sulfur product is basic.
4  Both solutions are acidic because both substances were burned in air.

Which statements are correct?

options.A: 1 and 2
options.B: 1 and 3
options.C: 2 and 4
options.D: 3 and 4

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Pooja burns sulfur powder in air. The product is sulfur dioxide. She dissolves it in water and tests the solution with litmus. Which claim is correct?

options.A: The solution is acidic and turns blue litmus red.

stem: Meena's teacher asks the class: 'We see metals everywhere — in our pressure cookers, cycles and ceiling fans. Are metals the only substances important in everyday life?' Which student gives the most correct answer?

options.D: Farah: Yes, because nitrogen is used to purify drinking water.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem:
Arjun tells his classmate Meera that only metals are useful in daily life because we see metal tools, wires, and machines everywhere. Meera disagrees and says non-metals are also essential.

Which example best supports Meera's argument that non-metals are essential in everyday life?

options.A: Steel spoons and aluminium utensils are used in the kitchen.
options.B: Copper wires carry electricity to fans and lights in homes.

subject: science
chapter_label: The world of metals and non-metals
stem: Naveen's teacher asks whether metals are the only substances important in everyday life, or whether non-metals such as oxygen, nitrogen, and chlorine also matter for breathing, fertilisers, and drinking water. Which reply is correct?

options.A: Non-metals are also essential: oxygen for breathing, nitrogen in fertilisers, and chlorine to purify drinking water.

options.C: Every non-metal is essential in everyday life.

options.A: Ice cubes melting in a glass of water
options.B: The steel spoon developing rust
options.C: Cutting the onion into small pieces

subject: science
stem:
In her home in Jaipur, Meena observes four changes.

options.A: W and X
options.B: X and Z
options.C: W and Y
options.D: Y and Z

rows: ice cubes melting in a glass of water
an iron gate forming rust in the rain

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 3 only
options.C: 2 and 3 only

statements.text: An iron nail left in damp air gets a brown flaky coat: a new substance has formed, so this is a chemical change.

Ice melts in a glass: a new substance has formed, so this is a chemical change.

stem: Firoz watches two changes. An iron nail left in damp air gets a brown flaky coat. Ice melts in a glass.

parts.text: Which claim correctly says whether a new substance has formed?

options.text: The nail’s brown coat is a new substance (chemical change); melting ice is not a new substance (physical change).
Melting ice forms a new substance (chemical change); the nail’s brown coat does not (physical change).
Both changes form a new substance because both look different afterward.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's teacher asks the class to find evidence that a gas produced during an experiment is carbon dioxide and that a chemical change has occurred.

Which observation is the best evidence for carbon dioxide causing a chemical change?

options.A: Bubbles escape when Rohan opens a bottle of soda water in the school canteen
options.B: Air blown through a straw into lime water turns the lime water milky
options.C: Water in a pan left on a hot stove slowly evaporates
options.D: A glass of cold water forms droplets on its outer surface on a humid day

subject: science
stem: Ritu blows through a straw into a glass of clear lime water in her kitchen at home. After some time, the lime water turns milky. Why is this milky appearance evidence that carbon dioxide is present and a chemical change has taken place?

options.A: The milkiness is a new insoluble substance, calcium carbonate, formed when carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide
options.B: The milkiness appears because carbon dioxide dissolves in the water and makes it cloudy
options.C: The milkiness shows that the water has evaporated when warm air is blown into it
options.D: The milkiness is calcium hydroxide settling down at the bottom of the glass

subject: science
stem:

Which claim correctly explains the milkiness as evidence for carbon dioxide and a chemical change?

options.A: Carbon dioxide reacted with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate.
options.B: The new white solid is calcium hydroxide.
options.C: Dissolved calcium carbonate made the lime water milky.
options.D: Calcium carbonate and water make calcium hydroxide and carbon dioxide.

subject: science
stem: Nikhil bubbles a gas through clear lime water. The lime water turns milky.

parts.text: What does the milky lime water show?

options.text: The gas is carbon dioxide, and a chemical change has formed a new white solid.
The gas is oxygen, and lime water always turns milky with any gas.
The milky look is only a physical mixing, so no chemical change has occurred.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: science
stem: Meena watches her mother light a wood fire in the chulha at home in Pune. Which observation shows that burning the wood is a combustion reaction?

options.A: The wood reacts with oxygen and gives out heat and light.
options.B: The wood changes its shape and size as it burns.
options.C: The ash left behind can be collected after burning.
options.D: The wood becomes hotter only because the weather is warm.

subject: science
stem:
During Diwali, Meera observes four different changes happening at home and notes them in her notebook.

She remembers that combustion is a reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen and produces heat or light.

Which of the changes Meera observed is combustion?

options.A: An electric bulb glowing and giving out heat when switched on
options.B: A piece of camphor burning in air with a flame during aarti
options.C: Wax melting near a hot diya and becoming soft
options.D: Water in a pan boiling and giving off steam on the stove

subject: science
stem: Harish checks whether a change is combustion: the substance must react with oxygen and produce heat or light. He compares camphor burning in air with a flame, a reaction with nitrogen, an oxygen-free heat-releasing reaction, and a flameless reaction with oxygen that releases heat. Which claim is correct?

options.A: Camphor burning in air with a flame is combustion.
options.B: Nitrogen is the gas required for combustion.
options.C: An oxygen-free reaction that releases heat is combustion.
options.D: A flameless reaction with oxygen that releases heat is not combustion.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Kiran burns a small piece of camphor in air. It reacts and produces a flame with heat and light.

parts.text: Is this change combustion?

options.text: Yes — the camphor reacts with oxygen and produces heat and light.
No — any bright change is combustion even when oxygen is not involved.
No — heat alone is enough to call a change combustion, with no reaction with oxygen.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: science
stem: Meena lights a small diya filled with ghee on her study table. It keeps burning steadily. Her brother then places a glass tumbler upside down over the diya, and after some time the flame goes out. Which statement correctly explains why the diya kept burning at first but later went out?

options.A: At first all three needs—ghee as fuel, oxygen from the air, and heat from lighting—were met; under the tumbler the fuel was finished, so the flame stopped.
options.B: At first all three needs—ghee as fuel, oxygen from the air, and heat above the ghee's ignition temperature—were met; under the tumbler the oxygen ran out, so burning stopped.
options.C: The diya kept burning because ghee alone is enough for combustion; under the tumbler the flame went out only because it could not be seen.
options.D: The diya kept burning because oxygen and fuel were present; heat is needed only to light it once and plays no further role in burning.

subject: science
stem:
Meena lights a diya filled with ghee and places it in a closed steel box with no air holes. After a short time, the flame goes out.

Why did the flame go out?

options.A: The ghee was not a combustible substance.
options.B: The ghee did not reach its ignition temperature.
options.C: The supply of oxygen inside the closed box was used up.
options.D: The steel box absorbed the ghee from the diya.

subject: science
stem:
Vivek lights a diya filled with ghee. It burns steadily. He then places a glass tumbler upside down over the diya, and after some time the flame goes out.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: At first ghee as fuel, oxygen from the air, and heat above the ghee's ignition temperature were all present; under the tumbler the oxygen ran out, so burning stopped.
options.B: The ghee caught fire as soon as it melted in air.
options.C: Once lit, the diya needs only ghee as fuel to keep burning; heat above ignition temperature is not needed for continued burning.
options.D: The covered diya keeps burning until the ghee runs out; oxygen is needed only to light it.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Wasim lights a candle. It burns steadily. He then covers the candle with a glass. After some time the flame goes out. He also finds that a wet paper strip does not catch fire from the same match as quickly as a dry paper strip.

parts.text: Which claim about starting and continuing burning is best?

options.text: Burning needs fuel, oxygen, and enough heat to reach ignition temperature; under the glass the oxygen runs low, and wet paper needs more heating to reach ignition.
Once lit, the candle needs only wax as fuel; oxygen and heat above ignition temperature are not needed for continued burning.
Wet paper fails to catch fire because paper is never a fuel, wet or dry.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

subject: science
stem:
Meena watches four things happening at home in Jaipur.

1. Ice cubes melt in a glass of water.
2. A candle burns on the table: some wax melts, and the wax vapour burns to form new substances.
3. Milk is boiled and then cooled in the fridge.
4. An iron nail left in the rain slowly rusts.

Which activity includes both a physical change and a chemical change?

subject: science
stem: Meera lights a diya filled with ghee during a festival. The ghee near the wick melts and turns to vapour, and the vapour then burns with a flame. Which statement about the burning diya is correct?

options.A: Only physical changes take place, because the melted ghee can solidify again.
options.B: Only a chemical change takes place, because a flame is seen.
options.C: The diya undergoes both a physical change, when ghee melts and evaporates, and a chemical change, when the ghee vapour burns to form new substances.
options.D: No change takes place, because the ghee is used up slowly.

subject: science
stem:
Rina watches a candle on the table: some wax melts, and the wax vapour burns to form new substances.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: This process includes both physical changes (melting) and a chemical change (burning vapour to new substances).
options.B: Melting wax and letting it solidify alone involves both physical and chemical changes.
options.C: Melting wax produces the heat that keeps the candle burning.
options.D: Evaporation of wax forms new substances.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Noor watches a candle: some solid wax melts, and the wax vapour burns and forms new substances.

parts.text: Which claim correctly describes the process?

options.text: The process includes both a physical change (melting) and a chemical change (burning vapour to new substances).
Melting wax and letting it solidify alone already includes both physical and chemical changes.
Melting wax produces the heat that keeps the candle burning.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera's mother melts some butter in a pan while cooking. When the melted butter is cooled, it becomes solid again.

The original substance ……1…… be brought back in its starting form.

So melting the butter is a ……2…… change.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 can; 2 non-reversible
options.B: 1 can; 2 reversible
options.C: 1 cannot; 2 reversible
options.D: 1 cannot; 2 non-reversible

subject: science
stem:

Which question helps her decide, and which change is reversible?

options.A: Ask: does the substance look different now? Both melting the wax and melting the chocolate are reversible.
options.B: Ask: can the original substance be brought back in its starting form? Both melted wax and melted chocolate can solidify back, so both changes are reversible.
options.C: Ask: can the original substance be brought back in its starting form? Melting the wax is reversible, but once something has changed it can never go back, so the chocolate is not reversible.
options.D: Ask: does the change happen quickly? Melting wax is slow so it is reversible; melting chocolate is quick so it is not reversible.

subject: science
stem:
Gauri melts some wax, then lets it cool until it is solid again. She also chops a carrot into pieces.

Which judgment about these changes is correct?

options.A: Melting the wax is reversible, because the wax can be brought back in its starting solid form.
options.B: Chopping the carrot is reversible, because the carrot material is still there.
options.C: Melting the wax is not reversible, because melted wax looks different from solid wax.
options.D: Both changes are reversible, because both happen in the kitchen.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meena's mother keeps leftover cooked rice in the refrigerator, but after three days the rice smells sour. Meena's friend says, "Souring of food is always an undesirable change." Using the situation and purpose, which statement is correct?

options.A: Souring of milk is always undesirable, so setting curd from milk at home is also undesirable.
options.B: The souring of the leftover rice is undesirable here because the rice was meant to be eaten later and is now spoilt.
options.C: The souring of the rice is desirable because every chemical change is useful.
options.D: The souring of the rice is neither desirable nor undesirable because a change cannot be judged.

subject: science
stem:

Which statements are correct?

1  Ripening of mangoes kept in a paper bag is desirable when the family wants to eat them soon.
2  Rusting of the iron gate is undesirable because it weakens the gate, even though rusting is a slow natural change.
3  The same change, such as the souring of milk, can be desirable when making curd but undesirable when the milk was meant for drinking.

options.A: 1, 2 and 3
options.B: 1 and 2 only
options.C: 1 and 3 only
options.D: 2 and 3 only

statements.text: Ripening of mangoes kept in a paper bag is desirable when the family wants to eat them soon.
Rusting of the iron gate is undesirable because it weakens the gate, even though rusting is a slow natural change.
The same change, such as the souring of milk, can be desirable when making curd but undesirable when the milk was meant for drinking.

options.B: Oxygen from air is essential for the leaf to prepare starch.
options.C: Water and sunlight are enough for the leaf to prepare starch without carbon dioxide.
options.D: Preparing starch produces the carbon dioxide around the leaf.

options.C: 2 and 3 only

B. Water and minerals travel from the leaves down to the roots through the xylem.

options.A: Water and minerals travel from the roots to the leaves through the phloem
options.B: Water and minerals travel from the leaves down to the roots through the xylem

options.D: Water and minerals are carried by the xylem to the leaves only, and never reach the flowers

options.D: Through xylem, from roots toward leaves only, not flowers.

options.C: Glucose releases carbon dioxide, water, and energy even when no oxygen is available.
options.D: Only green parts carry out respiration; non-green roots do not.

options.D: Only green plant parts respire; non-green roots do not.

subject: science
stem: Meera's teacher asks her to explain why the broad, flat leaves of the money plant growing near her classroom window are good at making food. Which answer correctly justifies this?

options.B: A broad, flat shape makes the leaf heavier, so it can store more water for making food
options.C: A broad, flat shape helps the leaf take in more soil minerals directly from the air

subject: science
stem:

subject: science
stem: Priya wants to find out whether warm or cold conditions change the speed at which water travels up a plant stem. She has two similar hibiscus twigs cut from the same plant, two identical glasses, and some red ink. Which plan is a fair test of her question?

options.A: Put both twigs in glasses with equal amounts of red ink water; keep one glass in a warm sunny window and the other in a cool fridge; record which twig shows red colour in its leaves first.
options.B: Put a long twig in red ink water in the warm window and a short twig in plain water in the fridge; record which twig shows red colour first.
options.C: Put one hibiscus twig in red ink water in the warm window and one rose twig in red ink water in the fridge; record which twig shows red colour first.
options.D: Put both twigs in the warm window, one in a glass with a little red ink and one in a glass full of red ink; record which twig shows red colour first.

subject: science
stem:

She places two similar cut hibiscus twigs in glasses of red-coloured water.
Which plan is a fair test?

options.A: Put one twig in a warm room and the other in a cold room, keeping the amount of coloured water, the size of the twigs and the light the same in both.
options.B: Put a long twig in cold water and a short twig in warm water, then see which twig turns red at the top first.
options.C: Put one twig in red ink and the other in plain water, both in the same warm room, then compare the colours.
options.D: Put a rose twig in the sun and a mango twig in the shade, then measure how much water each one absorbs.

options.B: Put a short twig in the warm place and a long twig in the cold place, then see which turns red first.
options.C: Use only a twig without flowers, because a twig with flowers cannot show water transport.
options.D: Choose the twig whose leaves look darkest red, even if those leaves turned red later.

Which observations could count as evidence of what happened during the experiment?

options.B: 1, 3 and 4

options.D: 3 only

Meera is making chapati dough in her kitchen. She notices that dough kept in a warm corner of the kitchen rises faster than dough kept near the window. Her mother says, "Now you have your answer — warmth helps the dough rise."

Meera writes down what she saw and then asks, "Does the type of flour also change how fast the dough rises?" She plans a new test.

Which statement best explains why Meera's careful observation is useful for science?

options.A: Her observation ends the investigation because one clear answer has been found.
options.B: Her observation provides evidence for one explanation and also opens a new question for further testing.
options.C: Her observation is not scientific because it was made in a kitchen and not in a laboratory.
options.D: Her observation counts as evidence only because it agrees with what her mother already believed.

stem: In her school science class in Pune, Meera observes an Amoeba (a single cell) under the microscope, while her classmate Arjun sketches a neem plant (made of many cells). Which of the following statements about how living organisms are built from cells is correct: () A. Only large organisms like the neem plant are made of cells, while tiny organisms like Amoeba are not made of cells; B. All living organisms are made of cells, whether they have one cell like Amoeba or many cells like the neem plant; C. Only organisms with many cells can carry out life processes, so a single cell cannot be a complete organism; D. Cells are found only in plants and animals, and not in microorganisms

options.A: Only large organisms like the neem plant are made of cells, while tiny organisms like Amoeba are not made of cells
options.B: All living organisms are made of cells, whether they have one cell like Amoeba or many cells like the neem plant
options.C: Only organisms with many cells can carry out life processes, so a single cell cannot be a complete organism

stem:

Which main cell part does the first job?

options.A: The cytoplasm, because many life processes occur there.
options.B: The cell membrane, because it controls what enters and leaves and separates cells.
options.C: The nucleus, because it regulates the cell’s activities and growth.
options.D: The cell membrane, because controlling materials in and out also means it regulates the cell’s growth.

options.B: The cytoplasm does the second job: many life processes occur there.
options.C: The nucleus does the first job: it controls what enters and leaves and separates cells.
options.D: The cell membrane does the third job as well, because controlling materials in and out means it regulates growth.

stem: In her school laboratory, Meena observes two cells under a microscope during a biology practical in Pune. Cell P is thin and flat, forming a protective lining on the inside of the cheek. options.B: Cell P is long and branched so it can carry messages, while Cell Q is thin and flat so it can form a protective lining.

options.D: The long, branched shape helps the cell move food.

subject: science
stem:
Ravi looked at a drop of pond water under a microscope in his school laboratory in Patna. He saw a tiny Amoeba moving about, feeding and reproducing, all on its own.
Ravi said, "It has only one cell, so it cannot be a complete living organism."
Which statement about the Amoeba is correct?

options.A: It is a complete living organism because one cell carries out all the functions needed for survival.
options.B: It is not a living organism because all living organisms are made of many cells.
options.C: It is alive only when it joins with other Amoeba cells to form a group.
options.D: It is a complete organism only because it lives in pond water.

subject: science
stem: During a science class in Meerut, Riya looks at a drop of pond water under the microscope and sees a single-celled Amoeba moving and feeding on its own. Her classmate Arjun says, “It has only one cell, so it cannot be a complete living organism.” Which statement is correct?

options.A: Arjun is correct, because every living organism must be made of many cells.
options.B: Riya is correct to disagree, because the single cell of an Amoeba carries out all life processes, so it is a complete organism.
options.C: Arjun is correct, because unicellular organisms can feed but cannot reproduce on their own.
options.D: Neither is correct, because an Amoeba becomes a complete organism only after joining with other cells.

subject: science
stem:
Ritu looks at an Amoeba under a microscope. It moves, feeds, and reproduces on its own. A classmate says it cannot be a complete living organism because it has only one cell. Bacteria are also single-celled microorganisms.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The Amoeba is a complete living organism because its one cell carries out all functions needed for survival.
options.B: A cell taken from a multicellular organism is itself a complete organism.
options.C: All microorganisms are unicellular like this Amoeba.
options.D: A bacterium is an incomplete living organism because it has only one cell.

stem: Meera collects a drop of pond water and a pinch of moist soil mixed in water for her class project. Under a microscope she sees many tiny moving beings, but she can see nothing in these samples with her unaided eye. What should she conclude about these tiny moving beings?

options.A: They are microorganisms, because they are living beings too small to be seen with the unaided eye.
options.B: They are not microorganisms, because the pond water and soil look like plain dirt to the unaided eye.
options.C: They are not microorganisms, because microorganisms are found only in water and never in moist soil.
options.D: They are not microorganisms, because anything that moves under a microscope must be a non-living particle.

stem: Meena collects a few drops of water from a pond near her school in Jaipur. To her unaided eye, the water looks clear with nothing living in it. Under a foldscope, she sees many tiny moving specks that she could not see before. What should Meena conclude about these tiny moving specks?

options.A: They are not living beings, because clear pond water cannot contain any organisms.

options.C: They are microorganisms, because they are tiny living beings that can only be seen with magnification.
options.D: They are large insects, because only insects can live in pond water.

options.A: A nonliving soil grain seen only under the microscope is a microorganism.
options.B: The tiny beings are microorganisms, because they are living and too small for the unaided eye.
options.C: Microorganisms occur only in the pond water, not in the moist soil.
options.D: The tiny living beings that stay still are not microorganisms.

options.A: bacterium

Meera keeps four bowls of cooked dal on the kitchen table in her home in Pune for two days. The table shows the condition of each bowl.
In which bowl are microorganisms most likely to grow and spoil the dal?

options.A: dal mixed with a large amount of salt
options.B: plain dal left uncovered in warm air
options.C: dal mixed with a large amount of sugar
options.D: dal kept covered in the refrigerator

subject: science
stem: Meena left a bowl of cooked dal uncovered on the kitchen counter, and by the next morning it had turned sour. Beside it, a jar of mango pickle made with plenty of salt and oil stayed fresh for many months. Which statement best explains why the dal rotted but the pickle did not get infected in the same way?

options.A: The dal rotted because it was naturally weak, while the pickle stayed safe simply because it is a pickle.
options.B: Microorganisms from the air and surroundings settled on the exposed dal and made it rot, while the high salt in the pickle acted as a preservative that prevented microbial infection.
options.C: The dal rotted first and the rotting itself produced the microorganisms that soured it.
options.D: Only a large amount of salt or sugar can stop microorganisms, so the small amount of salt in the pickle played no role in keeping it fresh.

subject: science
stem:

Which statement best explains why the dal spoils but the pickle does not get infected in the same way?

options.A: Microorganisms from the air settle on the exposed dal and spoil it, while enough salt in the pickle acts as a preservative.
options.B: Even a tiny amount of salt would keep the dal from spoiling.
options.C: The dal rots first, and that rotting produces the microorganisms.
options.D: The pickle cannot get infected, even without enough salt, because it is a pickle.

options.C: The warm water alone produces gas in any dough left for one hour.

stem:

Why does the dough with yeast rise?

options.A: Yeast is a microorganism that grows in the warm dough and makes the dough rise after some time.
options.B: Warm water and flour rise on their own, so the yeast is not needed at all.
options.C: Yeast is only a flavouring powder and the sugar alone makes the dough rise.
options.D: The dough rises first, which then gives the yeast enough room to grow in it.

subject: science
stem:
Sahil prepares two balls of dough with flour, sugar, and warm water. He adds yeast to the first ball and leaves yeast out of the second. After one hour, only the first ball has risen.

Why does the dough with yeast rise while the dough without yeast does not?

options.A: The yeast dough rises immediately when the yeast is mixed in.
options.B: Yeast grows in the warm dough and makes the dough rise after some time.
options.C: The dough must expand first to give the yeast room to grow.
options.D: Both doughs stay the same size later because they look identical just after mixing.

options.B: The microorganisms in the curd starter grow and multiply faster at warm temperatures, turning the milk into curd.
options.C: Both bowls form curd equally fast, so the difference is only in how sour they taste.
options.D: Warmth kills the microorganisms in the starter, so lukewarm milk sets while cold milk stays liquid.

subject: science
stem: Priya's mother mixes a spoonful of curd into two bowls of milk. Bowl 1 has warm milk; bowl 2 has milk straight from the refrigerator. After five hours, only bowl 1 has set into firm curd. What is the best reason for this difference?

options.A: The bacteria in the starter grow and multiply faster at warm temperatures, so they turn the milk into curd quickly.
options.B: Cold milk contains fewer nutrients, so the bacteria in the starter cannot use it.
options.C: Warmth kills all the harmful microorganisms in the milk, allowing curd to form.
options.D: The refrigerator adds extra water to the milk, which stops curd from setting.

stem:

Which statement best explains this difference?

options.A: Microorganisms in the curd starter grow and multiply faster in lukewarm milk, turning it into curd.
options.B: Lukewarm milk turns into curd immediately when the starter is mixed in.
options.C: Only the cold milk forms curd; lukewarm milk stays liquid because warmth stops the starter.
options.D: Both bowls have formed curd because both can taste a little sour.

options.B: Microalgae supply nitrogen to the air instead of oxygen when they make food using sunlight.
options.C: Microalgae can keep making their own food by the same process even in permanent darkness.

options.B: Setup 1, because it has two electrodes of different metals and the lemon juice acts as an electrolyte
options.C: Setup 4, because iron is a better conductor than copper
options.D: Setup 3, because keeping the electrodes dry makes the cell safer and stronger

stem:

Which setup is a working Voltaic cell?

options.C: One copper strip and one iron strip in the lemon, connected by wires to the LED — this is a dry cell.
options.D: The LED must glow first, and that glow then makes the copper and iron strips in the lemon into a cell.

options.B: a dry cell, because its electrolyte is a paste and it is convenient for daily use

Which statement about the dry cell is correct?

options.A: It contains a liquid electrolyte that can spill easily, so it is best for the portable torch.
options.B: Its electrolyte is held as a moist paste, so it can be carried and used conveniently in everyday devices.
options.C: It is called dry because it contains no electrolyte at all inside it.
options.D: It must always be kept in one fixed position, so it is less convenient than a Voltaic cell.

stem:

options.B: It is a rechargeable cell because it can be recharged and reused many times.
options.C: It is a single-use cell because it is used inside a torch.

options.A: A battery is rechargeable if it gives a large current the first time it is used.
options.B: A battery is rechargeable if it can be connected to a charger and used again for many cycles.
options.C: A battery is rechargeable if it is small and light enough to fit inside a torch.
options.D: A battery is rechargeable if it stops working completely after one use.

options.C: The force had no effect because the trolley was at rest.

subject: science
stem:

Which claim about these forces is correct?

options.A: A force between her hands and the ball can change the ball's shape, and a force between her hand and the book can start the book moving.
options.B: A force between objects counts only when it starts an object moving from rest.

options.A: Both are contact forces, because in both cases something makes the object move.

subject: science

options.A: Friction acts only after the box has stopped, so it pulls the box backwards on the wooden table.

subject: science
stem:
Meera fills a tall plastic bottle with water and makes three small holes at different heights on the side of the bottle. Water spurts out from each hole.
What does this show about the pressure exerted by the water?

options.A: Water exerts pressure only downward on the bottom of the bottle.
options.B: Water exerts pressure on the side walls of the bottle, and this pressure increases with depth.
options.C: Water exerts pressure only when the bottle is shaken.
options.D: Water exerts equal pressure at every point in the bottle.

subject: science
stem:
Farhan fills a tall plastic bottle with water and closes the cap. He then makes a small hole in the side wall of the bottle, near the bottom.

What does he observe, and what does it show about the pressure exerted by the water?

options.A: Water flows out through the hole, showing that water also pushes on the side walls of the bottle.
options.B: No water comes out, showing that water pushes only downward on the bottom of the bottle.
options.C: No water comes out, because the closed cap stops water from pushing on the side wall.
options.D: Water flows out through the hole, showing that water pushes on the side walls only near the bottom.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Devansh fills a closed plastic bottle with water. He makes a small hole in the side wall near the bottom. Water streams out sideways through the hole.

Which claims are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Water flowing out the side hole shows that the liquid pushes on the side walls as well as downward.
options.B: A fluid in a closed container exerts pressure on the bottom and on the side walls.
options.C: Water pushes only straight down on the bottom, so a side hole cannot release water.
options.D: The closed cap alone stops all pressure on the side walls.

subject: science
stem:
Meena presses a rubber sucker hook onto a smooth steel almirah in her kitchen, and it stays firmly in place. Her brother says it sticks because rubber is naturally sticky. Meena says air pressure is responsible.
Which statement correctly explains why the sucker sticks?

options.A: The rubber surface is sticky, so it grips the steel; air pressure plays no role.
options.B: Pressing the sucker pushes air out, so the higher atmospheric pressure outside presses it against the steel.
options.C: Air pressure inside the sucker increases and pushes it onto the steel.
options.D: The steel almirah attracts the rubber sucker like a magnet attracts iron.

subject: science
stem:
Meena presses a rubber sucker hook onto a smooth glass window in her kitchen. After she pushes out the air from inside the sucker, it stays firmly attached to the glass.
Why does the sucker stick to the glass?

options.A: The rubber of the sucker is sticky and glues itself to the glass.
options.B: The atmospheric pressure outside the sucker is greater than the pressure inside it.
options.C: The glass pulls the sucker towards it with a magnetic force.
options.D: The weight of the sucker is too small for it to fall down.

subject: science
stem:
Ekta presses a rubber sucker onto a smooth steel cupboard. After she pushes air out from under the sucker, it stays firmly in place.

Why does the sucker stick?

options.A: The air pressure outside the sucker is greater than the air pressure under it, so the outside air presses it against the steel.
options.B: The atmospheric pressure outside sticks the sucker to the steel even when air was not pushed out from under it.
options.C: The air pressure under the sucker is greater than the air pressure outside, so the inside air presses it against the steel.
options.D: The sucker sticks even when the air pressure outside equals the air pressure under it.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in Jaipur, Ravi opens a window of his classroom. The air pressure inside the room is higher than the air pressure outside, and the two regions are connected through the open window.
Which statement about the air flow is correct?

options.A: Air flows from outside into the room because air moves from lower pressure to higher pressure.
options.B: Air flows from the room to the outside, and it flows faster when the pressure difference is larger.
options.C: Air does not flow at all because the pressure difference keeps the air at rest.
options.D: Air flows from outside into the room, and a larger pressure difference makes the flow slower.

subject: science
stem:
Meena opens the window of her warm kitchen. The air pressure inside the kitchen is higher than the air pressure outside, and the window is open so air can move between the two regions.
What happens to the air?

options.A: Air flows from outside to inside, and the flow gets faster as the pressure difference gets smaller.
options.B: Air flows from inside to outside, and a larger pressure difference makes the air flow faster.
options.C: Air flows from outside to inside, and a larger pressure difference makes the air flow faster.
options.D: Air does not move, because air only moves when it is first pushed by a fan or wind.

subject: science
stem:
Dhruv opens a window of his warm kitchen. The air pressure inside the kitchen is higher than the air pressure outside, and the open window connects the two regions.

What happens to the air?

options.A: Air flows from the kitchen to the outside, and a larger pressure difference makes the flow faster.
options.B: Air flows from the outside into the kitchen, and a larger pressure difference makes the flow faster.
options.C: Air flows from the kitchen to the outside, and the flow speed stays the same no matter how large the pressure difference is.
options.D: Air flows from the kitchen to the outside even if the window is closed and no path connects the two regions.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, strong wind blows fast over the tin roof of Meena's house in a village near Pune. The roof is lifted upward.
Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure, so the higher pressure of the still air inside the house pushes the roof upward.
options.B: The fast-moving air above the roof has higher pressure, and this higher pressure pushes the roof upward from outside.
options.C: The pressure of the fast-moving air above the roof is the same as the pressure inside, so the roof lifts only because of its own weight.
options.D: The pressure above the roof is lower simply because it is higher up, whether the air is moving or still.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, strong wind blows fast over the sloping tin roof of Meena's house in Pune.
The air inside the house below the roof is still.
Why can the roof be lifted off?

options.A: The fast wind pushes the roof directly upwards from above.
options.B: The fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure, so the higher air pressure below the roof pushes it up.
options.C: The still air inside the house has lower pressure than the fast-moving air above.
options.D: The wind increases the pressure equally on both sides of the roof, making it lighter.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, strong wind blows fast over the tin roof of Farhan's house. The air inside the house below the roof is still.

Why can the roof be lifted?

options.A: The fast-moving air above the roof has lower pressure, so the higher pressure of the still air below pushes the roof upward.
options.B: The fast-moving air above the roof has higher pressure, so that higher pressure pushes the roof upward from above.
options.C: The roof lifts even when the pressure of the still air below equals the pressure of the fast-moving air above.
options.D: The pressure above the roof is lower simply because it is above, whether the air is moving or still.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in her village in Rajasthan, Meena watches dark thunderstorm clouds build up over the heated fields. Her teacher asks her to explain how the heated land and the moist air above it produce a thunderstorm.
Which chain of events correctly explains the formation of the thunderstorm?

options.A: Rain clouds become heavy with water and simply fall down as rain.
options.B: Cool air sinks over the fields, creating high pressure that pushes the rain out of the clouds.
options.C: Moist air rises, cools and condenses into clouds, but no air flows in from surrounding areas.
options.D: The hot land warms the moist air above it; the warm air rises and creates a low-pressure region; cooler air flows in from surrounding high-pressure regions; the rising air cools and its water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon in a village in Rajasthan, Meena notices dark thunderclouds forming over the heated fields near her home.
Which sequence correctly explains how the thunderstorm develops?

options.A: Rain clouds become heavy and simply fall to the ground as rain.
options.B: The heated land warms the moist air above it, the warm air rises creating a low-pressure area, cooler air flows in, and the rising moist air cools and condenses into clouds and rain.
options.C: Cool air from the surroundings sinks over the fields, pushes the warm air down, and squeezes rain out of the clouds.
options.D: The sun heats the clouds directly until the water vapour in them turns into rain.

subject: science
stem:
On a hot afternoon, Chitra watches dark thunderstorm clouds build over heated fields. The air above the fields is warm and moist.

Which sequence correctly explains how the thunderstorm develops?

options.A: Heated land warms the moist air; the warm air rises and creates low pressure; cooler air flows in; the rising air cools and its water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.
options.B: Warm moist air warms the heated land; the land rises and creates low pressure; cooler air flows in; water vapour condenses into clouds and rain.
options.C: Heated land warms dry air; the dry air rises and creates low pressure; cooler air flows in; clouds and rain form without moist air.
options.D: The same chain produces a thunderstorm even when the air above the fields is cool and dry.
