subject: science
stem:
During a monsoon storm over her village in Kerala, Meera watches lightning flash and then hears thunder a few moments later.
Her teacher asks her to describe what happens inside the storm cloud, in the correct order.
Which sequence is correct?

options.A: Thunder is produced first, and the sound of thunder then causes the cloud's charges to separate and form lightning.
options.B: Rubbing between water droplets and ice particles separates charges in the cloud, the charge buildup breaks down the insulating property of air, a sudden discharge produces lightning, and the rapid heating and expansion of air produces thunder.
options.C: Lightning occurs when two clouds physically collide, and thunder is the sound of the clouds crashing into each other.
options.D: The rapid heating of air produces thunder first, and the vibration of the air then pulls charges apart to create lightning.

subject: science
stem:
During a monsoon storm over her school in Nagpur, Meera sees a bright flash of lightning and soon hears thunder. Inside the storm cloud, strong winds make water droplets and ice particles rub against each other.
Which sequence correctly describes how lightning and thunder are produced?

options.A: Rubbing separates charges; charge separation builds an imbalance; the built-up charge breaks down the insulating property of air; a sudden discharge gives lightning; rapid heating and expansion of air gives thunder.
options.B: Thunder heats the cloud first; the heat separates the charges; the charges then cancel each other quietly; the cloud collapses to give the lightning flash.
options.C: Two clouds physically collide; the collision directly produces the lightning flash; the flash then separates the charges; thunder comes from the clouds breaking apart.
options.D: Air first becomes a perfect conductor; charges flow slowly and silently; the silent flow produces thunder; thunder then ignites the lightning flash.

subject: science
stem:
During a storm, Ekta sees a bright flash of lightning and soon hears thunder. Inside the storm cloud, strong winds make water droplets and ice particles rub against each other.

Which sequence correctly describes how lightning and thunder are produced?

options.A: Rubbing separates charges; the charge buildup breaks down the insulating property of air; a sudden discharge gives lightning; rapid heating and expansion of air gives thunder.
options.B: Thunder is produced first; the sound of thunder then separates the charges and forms lightning.
options.C: Rubbing separates charges and lightning flashes even when the charge buildup is too small to break down the insulating property of air.
options.D: Ice particles alone separate the charges; water droplets play no part in the sequence.

options.C: forms equally over cold ocean water; eye is calm while surrounding regions have strong winds
options.D: forms equally over cold ocean water; eye has the strongest winds while surrounding regions are calm

stem:

Which row of the table correctly describes the formation of the cyclone and the conditions in its eye compared with the surrounding region?

options.A: Warm moist air rises over the warm ocean and water vapour condenses; the eye is a calm, lowest-pressure region while surrounding areas have strong winds and heavy rain
options.B: Warm moist air rises over the warm ocean and water vapour condenses; the eye has the strongest winds and heaviest rain of the whole storm
options.C: Cyclones form just as readily over cold ocean water; the eye is a calm, lowest-pressure region while surrounding areas have strong winds and heavy rain
options.D: Cold dry air sinks over the warm ocean to start the storm; the eye is calm but at the highest pressure in the storm

subject: science
stem:
Farhan reads about a large storm that forms over warm ocean water. Warm moist air rises, water vapour condenses into raindrops, and a lowest-pressure centre called the eye develops.

Which statement correctly describes the cyclone and its eye?

options.A: It forms over warm ocean water; the eye is calm while surrounding regions have strong winds and heavy rain.
options.B: It forms over warm ocean water; winds are calm throughout the cyclone, including the region around the eye.
options.C: It forms just as readily over cold ocean water; the eye is calm while surrounding regions have strong winds and heavy rain.
options.D: It forms over warm ocean water; rising water vapour evaporates into raindrops, and the eye is calm.

burning a piece of paper to ash
water evaporating from a hot plate

subject: science
stem: Priya grinds a piece of chalk into a fine powder and then stirs some sugar into a glass of water until it can no longer be seen. Which statement best explains what has happened to the chalk and the sugar?

options.A: The chalk and sugar have become nothing, because no large pieces can be seen.
options.B: The chalk and sugar are still present as extremely small particles that are too small to see.
options.C: The sugar has disappeared, but the chalk has changed into a new substance.
options.D: Grinding and dissolving destroy the particles of a substance completely.

subject: science
stem:
Harish crushes a lump of rock salt into fine grains. He then stirs some of those grains in a glass of water until they can no longer be seen.

Which statement best explains what has happened to the rock salt?

options.A: The rock salt has become nothing, because no grains can be seen.
options.B: The rock salt is still present as extremely small particles that are too small to see.
options.C: Crushing and dissolving destroy every particle of the rock salt.
options.D: The rock salt has changed into something that was never salt.

options.B: The rock salt is still present as extremely small particles that are too small to see.
options.C: Crushing and dissolving destroy every particle of the rock salt.

stem: Meera stirs a spoonful of sugar into a glass of water until no sugar grains can be seen, yet the water still tastes sweet. Which statement best explains what has happened to the sugar?

options.A: The sugar particles have disappeared, and only the sweetness is left in the water.
options.B: The sugar particles have separated and spread into the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.C: The sugar has melted into liquid sugar, which sits at the bottom of the glass.
options.D: Each sugar particle has gone inside a water particle, making the water particles sweet.

subject: science
stem:
Meena adds two spoons of sugar to a glass of water and stirs. After some time, no sugar grains can be seen, yet the whole glass of water tastes sweet.

Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The sugar particles spread out and occupy the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.B: The sugar particles melt into a liquid and float on top of the water, making it sweet.
options.C: The sugar disappears completely, and only its sweetness stays behind in the water.
options.D: Each water particle absorbs a sugar particle inside itself, which makes the water particle sweet.

subject: science
stem:
Uday stirs a spoon of sugar into a glass of water. Soon no sugar grains can be seen, yet the water tastes sweet throughout the glass.

Which statement best explains this?

options.A: The sugar particles spread into the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.B: The sugar particles gather only at the top of the water, and only that top layer tastes sweet.
options.C: The sugar vanishes completely, and only a sweet taste remains with no sugar particles left.
options.D: Each water particle takes a sugar particle inside itself, which makes that water particle sweet.

options.A: The sugar particles spread into the spaces between the water particles, so sugar is present throughout the water.
options.B: The sugar particles gather only at the top of the water, and only that top layer tastes sweet.
options.C: The sugar vanishes completely, and only a sweet taste remains with no sugar particles left.

stem:
Meera keeps a steel tiffin box on her study table. She notices that the tiffin box always keeps the same shape and the same size, no matter where she places it.

Why does a solid like the steel tiffin box have a definite shape and a definite volume?

options.A: Its particles are tightly packed and attract each other very strongly, so they stay in fixed positions and only vibrate.
options.B: Its particles are tightly packed, and this tight packing alone holds the shape even though the particles attract each other only weakly.
options.C: Its particles move freely throughout the box but the hard outer surface stops the box from changing shape.
options.D: The fixed shape and volume of the box push its particles close together and make their attractions strong.

options.A: 1 tightly packed; 2 very weak
options.B: 1 tightly packed; 2 very strong
options.C: 1 far apart; 2 very strong
options.D: 1 far apart; 2 very weak

subject: science
stem:

options.A: Its particles are tightly packed, and the attractions between them are very weak.
options.B: Its particles are tightly packed, and the attractions between them are very strong.
options.C: Its particles are far apart, and the attractions between them are very strong.
options.D: Its particles are far apart, and the attractions between them are very weak.

options.A: Its particles are tightly packed, and the attractions between them are very strong.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's mother places a piece of solid ghee in a pan and heats it gently. The ghee becomes a liquid.

Which statement best explains why the ghee melts, and how its melting point is identified?

options.A: Heating makes the particles vibrate more strongly until they can leave their fixed positions; the melting point is the lowest temperature, at atmospheric pressure, at which the solid ghee becomes a liquid.
options.B: Heating makes the particles stop vibrating so they can flow; the melting point is the temperature at which the liquid ghee begins to boil.
options.C: Heating creates new particles that fill the gaps; the melting point is any temperature listed for ghee in a table of data.
options.D: Heating makes the particles larger so they push apart; the melting point is the highest temperature the solid ghee can reach before burning.

subject: science
stem: Meera's mother keeps a block of jaggery near the hot stove, and after some time it starts turning soft and syrupy at its melting point. Which statement best explains why heating a solid like jaggery or ice can make it melt, and why the melting point is used to identify this change?

options.A: Heating pushes the particles closer together until they stop moving, and the melting point is the temperature at which particles stop vibrating.
options.B: Heating makes the particles vibrate more vigorously until they can leave their fixed positions, so the solid becomes liquid; the melting point is the specific temperature (at atmospheric pressure) at which this change begins, so it can be used to identify it.
options.C: Heating turns the solid particles into gas particles straight away, and the melting point is the temperature at which the solid evaporates.
options.D: Heating changes the particles into a different substance, and the melting point is just a number chosen from a table for each material.

subject: science
stem:
Soham heats a solid wax crayon. At its melting point the wax turns soft and liquid.

Which claim correctly explains melting and why the melting point identifies that change?

options.A: Heating makes the particles vibrate more until they leave fixed positions; the melting point is the temperature at which this change begins.
options.B: Heating pushes the particles closer until they stop vibrating; the melting point is when vibration stops.
options.C: Heating turns the solid straight into gas; the melting point is the boiling temperature.
options.D: Melting begins at any temperature once the crayon is stirred.

stem: Meena pours 200 mL of water from a bottle into a round bowl in her kitchen. The water spreads to take the shape of the bowl, but its volume stays 200 mL. Which statement correctly explains this?

options.A: The water particles break down into smaller particles when poured.
options.B: The water particles can move and change positions while attractions keep them close together.
options.C: The water particles are tightly fixed in one position and cannot move at all.
options.D: The water particles are far apart and move freely in all directions like a gas.

options.A: The particles in the milk are fixed in one position and cannot move at all.
options.B: The particles in the milk can move and change positions while staying close together because of the attraction between them.
options.C: The particles in the milk move freely in all directions and fill the whole glass.
options.D: The particles in the milk are far apart, so the milk can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

options.A: The particles in the oil are fixed in place and cannot move at all.
options.B: The particles in the oil can move and change positions while staying close because of the attraction between them.
options.C: The particles in the oil move freely in all directions and fill every part of the bowl.
options.D: The particles in the oil are far apart, so the oil can be squeezed into a smaller volume.

options.A: Gas particles have a fixed shape but move slowly, so the gas takes the shape of its container.
options.B: Gas particles move freely in all directions and the forces of attraction between them are negligible, so the gas spreads to fill all the available space.
options.C: Gas particles are tightly packed together, so the gas expands when the lid is opened.
options.D: Gas is mostly empty space, so steam spreads by itself without the particles needing to move.

stem: Priya adds a spoonful of sugar to a glass of water and stirs. Her brother Rohan adds a spoonful of sand to another glass of water and stirs. Why do the sugar and the sand affect the water in their glasses differently?

options.A: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles when they dissolve, but sand does not dissolve and its particles settle at the bottom.
options.B: Sugar particles disappear completely in water, but sand particles grow larger after stirring.
options.C: Sugar reacts with water to form a new substance, but sand evaporates when stirred.

subject: science
stem:
Priya adds one spoon of sugar to a glass of water and stirs until it disappears. The water level drops slightly below the mark she had made on the glass.

Her brother Rohan adds one spoon of sand to another identical glass of water and stirs. The sand settles at the bottom and the water level rises above the mark.

Why do the sugar and the sand affect the water level differently?

options.A: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles, but sand particles do not dissolve and take up space themselves.
options.B: All small solids behave in the same way when stirred into water, so the levels should be identical.
options.C: Sugar particles push the water particles apart, while sand particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
options.D: Sugar is heavier than sand, so it pulls the water level down, while sand floats and pushes the level up.

subject: science
stem:
Yash adds one spoon of sugar to a glass of water and stirs until it dissolves. In a second glass he adds one spoon of sand and stirs. The sugar water looks clear. The sand settles at the bottom.

Why do the two mixtures behave differently?

options.A: Sugar particles fit into spaces between water particles; sand does not dissolve, settles, and takes up space.
options.B: Sand dissolves the same way sugar does, so both glasses become clear after stirring.
options.C: Sugar dissolves even if Yash never stirs until it dissolves.
options.D: The water level falls first, and that fall causes the sugar to dissolve.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera's teacher places a few grains of potassium permanganate into a beaker of water. The colour slowly spreads through the water without any stirring.

Which statement correctly explains why the colour spreads and how using hotter water would change this?

options.A: The colour spreads because water particles are in constant motion, and the colour spreads faster in hotter water because the particles move faster.
options.B: The colour spreads only because the beaker is shaken, and the temperature of the water makes no difference.
options.C: The colour spreads because water particles are still, and the colour spreads more slowly in hotter water.
options.D: The colour spreads because the grains push the water aside, and hotter water stops the colour from spreading.

subject: science
stem: Meena adds a few drops of red food colouring to two identical glasses of water, one with cold water and one with hot water, without stirring either glass. Which statement about what she observes is correct?

options.A: The colour spreads only after Meena stirs the water with a spoon.
options.B: The colour spreads faster in the hot water because water particles move faster at higher temperature.
options.C: The colour spreads at the same rate in both glasses because water particles do not move.
options.D: The colour spreads faster in the cold water because cold water particles move faster.

subject: science
stem:
Eshan places a few grains of potassium permanganate in three glasses of water: ice-cold, room-temperature, and hot. He does not stir. Particles of liquids are in constant motion. Purple colour spreads through each glass, fastest in the hot water where particles move faster.

Which claim best explains this?

options.A: Water particles are in constant motion and move faster when hotter, so they spread the potassium permanganate particles most quickly in hot water.
options.B: The colour spreads only because the glasses are stirred, not because water particles move.
options.C: Hotter water spreads the colour more slowly because its particles move more slowly.
options.D: Only the potassium permanganate particles move; the water particles stay still in every glass.

subject: science
stem:
Priya lists four samples found in her home and school laboratory.

| sample | W | X | Y | Z |
| description | air in a balloon | pure distilled water | a brass (copper and zinc) plate | oxygen gas in a cylinder |

A mixture contains two or more substances physically mixed together, with each substance keeping its own properties. Which samples are mixtures?

options.A: W and X
options.B: W and Y
options.C: X and Z
options.D: Y and Z

subject: science
stem:
At home in Pune, Aarav makes jaljeera by stirring mint paste, roasted cumin powder, salt, lemon juice and chilled water in a steel jug. The drink looks cloudy, and he can still taste the lemon and mint separately. No gas bubbles or new solid appear.

Which check best decides whether the jaljeera is a mixture?

options.A: It is a mixture only if the liquid becomes one even colour throughout.
options.B: It is a mixture only if the substances react and form a new substance.
options.C: It is a mixture because two or more substances are physically mixed and each keeps its own properties.
options.D: It is not a mixture because the separate tastes can still be noticed.

subject: science
stem:
Lalit stirs sugar into water until the sugar dissolves. He can still taste the sugar. The water still feels wet.

Which claim about this sample is correct?

options.A: It is a mixture because sugar and water are physically mixed and each keeps its own properties.
options.B: It is a mixture only if sugar and water were pure substances before mixing.
options.C: It is not a mixture because the sugar can no longer be seen separately in the water.
options.D: It is not a mixture because the sugar's taste and the water's wetness can still be noticed.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Ojas stirs sugar into water until the sugar dissolves. He can still taste the sugar, and the water still feels wet. Separately, he mixes iron filings and sulphur powder that stay visible as two materials.

Which claims are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Sugar-water is a mixture because sugar and water are physically mixed and each keeps its own properties.
options.B: Iron filings with sulphur powder is a mixture because two substances are physically mixed and each keeps its own properties.
options.C: Sugar-water is not a mixture because the sugar can no longer be seen separately.
options.D: Iron filings with sulphur powder is not a mixture because both materials are solids.

subject: science
stem: Priya's mother makes a glass of nimbu pani (lemon water) by stirring lemon juice, sugar and salt into water until everything dissolves. Priya looks at the glass and cannot see the sugar, salt or lemon juice separately. How should Priya classify this mixture, and why?

options.A: Uniform mixture, because the components are spread evenly throughout and cannot be seen separately
options.B: Non-uniform mixture, because it contains more than one substance mixed together
options.C: Uniform mixture, because the lemon juice gives it one colour that can be seen
options.D: Non-uniform mixture, because the sugar is heavier than water and settles down

subject: science
stem: Meera is helping her mother in the kitchen. She prepares four mixtures. In which mixture are the components spread so evenly that they cannot be seen separately, even with a microscope?

options.A: Salt dissolved completely in a glass of water.

options.C: Mustard oil poured into a bowl of water.

options.A: Honey stirred completely into warm water until nothing separate can be seen.
options.B: Poha mixed with peanuts and green chilli pieces.
options.C: Mustard oil poured onto a bowl of water.
options.D: Chalk powder stirred into a bucket of water.

options.A: Honey stirred completely into warm water until nothing separate can be seen is a uniform mixture.

subject: science
stem:
Meena's teacher writes 'air' on the blackboard and asks the class how it should be classified. Meena knows that air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and that these gases are mixed together without chemically combining with one another.

How should air be classified?

options.A: A compound, because it contains more than one kind of substance
options.B: An element, because the gases in it keep their own properties
options.C: A mixture, because several gases are present together without being chemically combined
options.D: A pure substance, because it looks uniform and has no visible parts

Which statement best explains why air is a mixture?

options.A: Air is a mixture because it is invisible and looks the same everywhere in the room.
options.B: Air is a mixture because it contains several gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide that are physically mixed but not chemically combined into one substance.
options.C: Air is a mixture because two or more gases present together must react chemically and form a compound.
options.D: Air is not a mixture because the gases in it cannot be separated from one another.

Nalini lists the main gases in air: nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. These gases are not chemically combined into one substance.

Which claim about air is correct?

options.A: Air is a mixture because several gases are present together without a chemical change.
options.B: Air is a compound because several gases are present together.
options.C: Air is pure oxygen because living beings need oxygen.
options.D: Air is a mixture because separate gas layers can be seen.

Irfan lists the main gases in air: nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. These gases are not chemically combined into one substance.

Which claims are correct? One or more options may be correct.

options.A: Air is a mixture because several gases are present together without forming one new substance.
options.B: The gases in air keep their own properties and are not chemically combined.
options.C: Air is a compound because several gases are listed together.
options.D: Air is pure oxygen because living beings need oxygen.

Which gas in the air reacts with the lime water to make it turn milky?

options.B: nitrogen
options.C: carbon dioxide
options.D: water vapour

options.C: The salt cannot be a pure substance in science because it is sold in a shop.

options.A: distilled water, made of identical molecules each containing hydrogen and oxygen atoms

options.C: salt solution prepared by dissolving salt in water
options.D: sugar crystals, made of molecules containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms

Indira studies four pure samples: distilled water, made of identical molecules each containing hydrogen and oxygen; oxygen gas, made of identical molecules each containing only oxygen; carbon dioxide gas, made of identical molecules each containing carbon and oxygen; and sugar crystals, made of molecules containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. options.A: Distilled water, made of identical molecules each containing hydrogen and oxygen.
options.B: Oxygen gas, made of identical molecules each containing only oxygen.

subject: science
stem:
Chetan compares three classroom samples: water, a liquid made when hydrogen and oxygen are chemically joined into a compound whose properties differ from those separate elements; a dish of iron filings mixed with sulphur powder that a magnet can still pull apart as a mixture; and a strip of pure copper metal, an element that looks like one single solid piece of metal.

Which claim correctly classifies water?

options.A: Water is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically joined, and water's properties differ from those of the separate elements.
options.B: Water is a mixture: it contains more than one element, just as iron filings mixed with sulphur powder do.
options.C: Water is an element: it looks like one single liquid, as copper looks like one solid piece of metal.
options.D: Water is a compound even though hydrogen and oxygen keep their own separate properties inside it.

options.A: Water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen gases that can be separated by filtering.
options.B: Water is an element because it produces gases when electricity passes through it.
options.C: Water is a compound made of hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined together.
options.D: Water is a pure substance that contains only oxygen atoms.

subject: science
stem:
Wasim passes an electric current through water with a little dilute sulphuric acid. He collects two gases. One burns with a pop near a flame (hydrogen test); the other relights a glowing splint (oxygen test). Classmates debate element, compound, and mixture.

What do these results show about water?

options.A: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen chemically joined together.
options.B: Water is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen that can be separated without a chemical change.
options.C: Water is an element, because an electric current releases gases from it.
options.D: Water contains only oxygen, because a glowing splint can relight.

subject: science
stem: Meera heats some dry sugar in a dry boiling tube in her school laboratory. A black solid is left behind and droplets of water collect on the cooler parts of the tube. Which statement does not correctly use these observations to conclude that sugar is a compound?

options.A: The black solid is carbon, so sugar must contain the element carbon.
options.B: The water formed contains hydrogen and oxygen, so these elements must have come from the sugar.
options.C: The water droplets must have come from the air, so they tell us nothing about the elements in sugar.
options.D: Sugar breaks down on heating into simpler substances, which shows it is made of more than one element.

subject: science
stem:
Meera heats some sugar in a dry test tube in her school laboratory. She observes that a black solid is left behind and droplets of water collect on the cooler parts of the tube.

What does this experiment show about sugar?

options.A: Sugar is an element because it leaves behind only one black solid.
options.B: Sugar is a compound because it breaks down on heating to give carbon and water, showing it contains more than one element.
options.C: Sugar is a mixture because it gives two different products on heating.
options.D: Sugar is an element because the water droplets come from the sugar, not from the air.

subject: science
stem:
Amit heats dry sugar in a boiling tube. Water droplets form on the cooler upper part of the tube, and a black residue remains.

What does this show about sugar?

options.A: Sugar is a compound: heating decomposes it into carbon and water, so it contains more than one element.
options.B: Sugar is an element, because heating turns it brown and then black.
options.C: The water droplets came from the air, not from the dry sugar.
options.D: Sugar was already a mixture of carbon and water before heating.

stem:
For a school science project, Meena mixes iron filings with sulfur powder in a dish. Her brother Arjun heats a similar mixture strongly in a test tube to form iron sulfide.

Which statement correctly compares the iron and sulfur mixture with the iron sulfide formed after heating?

options.A: Both the mixture and the iron sulfide can be separated using a magnet, because both still contain iron.
options.B: The mixture shows yellow and grey particles and its iron is attracted by a magnet, while iron sulfide is a uniform black substance not attracted by a magnet.
options.C: The mixture and the iron sulfide react with dilute hydrochloric acid in exactly the same way, giving the same gas.
options.D: After heating, the black iron sulfide is still a mixture of iron and sulfur, so it keeps their original properties.

subject: science
stem:
For a school science activity, Priya mixes iron filings with powdered sulfur in a china dish at home. Her brother heats a similar sample strongly and obtains a black solid, iron sulfide.

Which observation shows that the unheated sample is a mixture and not the compound iron sulfide?

options.A: A magnet pulls the iron filings out of the unheated sample, but the heated black solid is not attracted to a magnet.
options.B: The unheated sample has one uniform colour throughout, just like the heated black solid.
options.C: Both the unheated sample and the heated black solid give the same gas with dilute hydrochloric acid.
options.D: The heated black solid can be separated back into iron and sulfur using a magnet.

Which comparison is correct?

options.A: Sample A shows black and yellow particles and a magnet attracts the iron; Sample B is a uniform black substance not attracted by a magnet.
options.B: Sample A and Sample B both attract a magnet in the same way.
options.C: Sample B still shows separate black and yellow particles like Sample A.
options.D: Sample A is a compound because iron and sulfur are present together.

stem:
Meera visits a geology exhibition in Jaipur with her class. She reads three display labels:

options.B: Granite – mixture; calcite – compound; native gold – pure element

Which classification is correct?

options.A: The rock is a mixture of minerals; the multi-element mineral is a compound; the native mineral is a pure element, not a compound.
options.B: The rock is a compound because several minerals sit together in one solid piece.
options.C: The native mineral is a compound because it is found in the Earth with other rocks.

options.C: Both solutions are equally concentrated because both use the same amount of water.
options.D: Neither solution is concentrated because salt always forms dilute solutions in water.

subject: science
stem:
Meena dissolves 4 spoons of sugar in 200 mL of water in a glass. Her brother Arjun dissolves 2 spoons of sugar in 200 mL of water in an identical glass. Both stir until all the sugar dissolves.

Which row correctly compares Meena's glass with Arjun's glass?

options.A: more sugar dissolved in the same amount of water: no; more concentrated: no
options.B: more sugar dissolved in the same amount of water: no; more concentrated: yes
options.C: more sugar dissolved in the same amount of water: yes; more concentrated: no
options.D: more sugar dissolved in the same amount of water: yes; more concentrated: yes

headers: more sugar dissolved in the same amount of water

subject: science
stem:
Padma dissolves 5 spoons of salt in 250 mL of water. Qasim dissolves 2 spoons of salt in 250 mL of water. Both stir until all the salt dissolves.

Which comparison is correct?

options.A: Padma has more solute in the same amount of solvent, so her solution is more concentrated.
options.B: Qasim has less solute, so his solution is more concentrated.
options.C: Both solutions have the same concentration because both use 250 mL of water.
options.D: Padma's solution is more concentrated because her glass looks fuller.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Jyoti dissolves 5 spoons of salt in 250 mL of water. Devansh dissolves 2 spoons of salt in 250 mL of water. Both stir until all the salt dissolves.

Which comparison is correct?

options.A: Jyoti has more solute in the same amount of solvent, so her solution is more concentrated.
options.B: Devansh has less solute, so his solution is more concentrated.
options.C: Both solutions have the same concentration because both use 250 mL of water.
options.D: Jyoti's solution is more concentrated because her glass looks fuller.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meena adds salt, a little at a time, to 100 mL of water in a glass, stirring after each addition. Which statement about her experiment is not correct?

options.A: The amount of salt that dissolves increases as more salt is added, at first.
options.B: The solubility of salt is the maximum amount that can dissolve in a fixed quantity of water.
options.C: If Meena keeps stirring long enough, the water can always dissolve more salt.
options.D: After the water has dissolved its maximum amount of salt, extra salt stays undissolved.

subject: science
stem: Meera is preparing salt water for a science activity at home in Jaipur. She adds spoonfuls of salt to 100 cm³ of water at room temperature, stirring after each spoonful. After a while, she notices that no matter how long she stirs, some salt stays at the bottom of the glass. What has happened to the water?

options.A: The salt has reacted with the water and formed a new substance.
options.B: The water has reached its solubility limit, so extra salt remains undissolved.
options.C: The water has evaporated, leaving the salt behind.
options.D: The salt particles have become too large to dissolve.

subject: science
stem:
Om adds salt little by little to a fixed amount of water at room temperature, stirring each time. After several additions, some salt stays undissolved at the bottom.

Which claim is correct?

options.A: The water has reached its dissolving limit for salt under these conditions.
options.B: The water will dissolve the remaining salt if Om only stirs longer, with no other change.
options.C: Solubility means the first amount of salt that dissolves, not the maximum.
options.D: Undissolved salt at the bottom means the water never dissolved any salt.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Priya adds baking soda to water at 20 °C in a steel tumbler at home. Some baking soda settles at the bottom and does not dissolve, even after stirring.

She then warms the mixture gently to 50 °C while stirring.

What will Priya most likely observe?

options.A: The undissolved baking soda dissolves, and more baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature.
options.B: The baking soda at the bottom turns into a new compound when warmed.
options.C: Heating only warms the water; the amount of baking soda that can dissolve stays the same.
options.D: The undissolved baking soda floats to the top and forms a separate layer.

subject: science
stem: Priya adds baking soda to water at 25 °C in a steel tumbler at home. Some baking soda settles at the bottom and does not dissolve. She then heats the mixture to 55 °C while stirring with a spoon. Which row correctly predicts what happens to the undissolved baking soda and to the amount of baking soda that can dissolve at the higher temperature?

options.A: undissolved baking soda remains at the bottom; the amount that can dissolve stays the same
options.B: undissolved baking soda dissolves; more baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature
options.C: undissolved baking soda dissolves; less baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature
options.D: undissolved baking soda remains at the bottom; the amount that can dissolve decreases

headers: amount that can dissolve at higher temperature

subject: science
stem:
Soham adds baking soda to water at about 20 °C. Some baking soda stays undissolved at the bottom. He heats the mixture to about 50 °C while stirring.

Which prediction is correct?

options.A: The undissolved baking soda dissolves, and more baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature.
options.B: The undissolved baking soda stays at the bottom, and the amount that can dissolve stays the same.
options.C: The undissolved baking soda dissolves, but less baking soda can dissolve at the higher temperature.
options.D: Heating only makes the water look cloudy; the amount that can dissolve does not change.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera notices that fish in the pond near her school in Chennai come to the surface more often on hot afternoons.

When water is warmed, the solubility of dissolved gases such as oxygen ……1…… .

This means warm water contains ……2…… dissolved oxygen than cold water.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 increases; 2 more
options.B: 1 increases; 2 less
options.C: 1 decreases; 2 more
options.D: 1 decreases; 2 less

subject: science
stem:
Meena notices that fish in her aquarium in Chennai come to the surface more often on very hot afternoons. She learns that water contains dissolved oxygen.

Which statements about dissolved oxygen in water are correct?

1  Cold water can hold more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
2  Warming water increases the amount of oxygen that can dissolve in it.
3  On hot days, fish may receive less oxygen from the water.
4  Dissolved oxygen forms a uniform solution in water.

options.A: 1, 2 and 4
options.B: 1, 3 and 4
options.C: 1 and 4 only
options.D: 4 only

statements.text: Cold water can hold more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
Warming water increases the amount of oxygen that can dissolve in it.
On hot days, fish may receive less oxygen from the water.
Dissolved oxygen forms a uniform solution in water.

subject: science
stem:
Om compares cold pond water and warm pond water. Fish need the dissolved oxygen in the water.

Which claim about dissolved oxygen is correct?

options.A: Cold water can hold more dissolved oxygen than warm water.
options.B: Warm water can hold more dissolved oxygen than cold water.
options.C: Water temperature does not affect how much oxygen dissolves, because only a small amount ever dissolves.
options.D: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen because warm water looks clearer.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera wants to find the density of a steel spoon she uses at home. She measures the mass of the spoon as 78 g and finds that it displaces 10 cm³ of water when fully immersed. Which calculation gives the correct density of the spoon?

options.D: 78 g, since the mass alone tells us the density

subject: science
stem:
Meera measures a steel spoon in her school laboratory. Its mass is 39 g and it displaces 5 cm³ of water in a measuring cylinder.

Which statements about the density of the spoon are correct?

1  Density is calculated as mass divided by volume.
2  Its density can be expressed in g/cm³.
3  Density is calculated as volume divided by mass.
4  Another spoon of the same volume but greater mass would have greater density.

options.A: 1 and 2 only
options.B: 1 and 4 only
options.C: 1, 2 and 4
options.D: 2, 3 and 4

statements.text: Density is calculated as mass divided by volume.
Its density can be expressed in g/cm³.
Density is calculated as volume divided by mass.
Another spoon of the same volume but greater mass would have greater density.

subject: science
stem:
Uday finds that a metal bolt has mass 48 g and displaces 6 cm³ of water in a measuring cylinder.

What is the density of the bolt?

options.A: 8 g/cm³
options.B: 0.125 g/cm³
options.C: 54 g/cm³
options.D: 288 g/cm³

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meera wants to find the density of a stone at home in Jaipur. She will measure its mass and its volume, then calculate density.

Which procedure should she follow before using her measurements?

options.A: Read the balance without checking the zero, then pour any amount of water into the measuring cylinder
options.B: Zero the balance before measuring the mass, then read the water level in the measuring cylinder at eye level before and after adding the stone
options.C: Measure the volume first and guess the mass by holding the stone in her hand
options.D: Use the highest mark on the measuring cylinder as the volume of the stone

subject: science
stem:
Meena wants to find the density of a small steel spoon at home. She first measures its mass on a digital weighing balance, then finds its volume using a measuring cylinder partly filled with water.

Which procedure should she follow before using her readings to calculate density?

options.A: Press the tare button so the balance reads zero before placing the spoon, and read the water level at the bottom of the meniscus.
options.B: Place the spoon on the balance straight away and read the number shown, and read the water level at the top of the meniscus.
options.C: Press the tare button so the balance reads zero before placing the spoon, and read the water level at the top of the meniscus.
options.D: Place the spoon on the balance straight away and read the number shown, and read the water level at the bottom of the meniscus.

subject: science
stem:
Wasim wants the density of a small steel nut. He will measure its mass on a digital balance and its volume with a measuring cylinder partly filled with water. He can press tare on the balance and must choose how to read the meniscus.

Which procedure should he follow before using the readings?

options.A: Press tare so the balance reads zero before placing the nut, and read the water level at the bottom of the meniscus.
options.B: Place the nut on the balance straight away, and read the water level at the top of the meniscus.
options.C: Press tare so the balance reads zero before placing the nut, and read the water level at the top of the meniscus.
options.D: Place the nut on the balance straight away, and read the water level at the bottom of the meniscus.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Priya is finding the volumes of four objects in her school laboratory.

Which objects should have their volumes found by water displacement in a measuring cylinder, not by a shape formula?

| object | W | X | Y | Z |
| description | iron cube of side 3 cm | piece of stone | wooden block 5 cm × 2 cm × 4 cm | broken piece of brick |

options.A: W and X
options.B: X and Z
options.C: W and Y
options.D: Y and Z

subject: science
stem:
Priya wants to find the volume of an irregularly shaped stone she found near the river. She has a measuring cylinder partially filled with water.

How should she find the volume of the stone?

options.A: Use the formula volume = length × width × height, treating the stone as a cuboid.
options.B: Lower the stone into the water and subtract the initial water reading from the final water reading.
options.C: Weigh the stone on a balance, since the mass is equal to the volume.
options.D: Read the water level in the cylinder before putting the stone in.

subject: science
stem:
Zara has a wooden cuboid with measurable length, width, and height. Amit has an irregular stone. Each needs the volume of their object. A measuring cylinder with water is available.

Which choice matches the correct volume method for each object?

options.A: Cuboid: length × width × height. Stone: final water reading minus initial water reading.
options.B: Cuboid: final water reading minus initial water reading. Stone: length × width × height.
options.C: Cuboid: length × width × height, even without measuring length, width, and height.
options.D: Both objects must use water displacement, because volume is found only that way.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: In her school laboratory, Meena measures the density of mustard oil as 0.91 g/cm³. The density of water at the same temperature is 1.0 g/cm³. She divides the two values to find the relative density of the oil. Which statement about the relative density is correct?

options.A: It is 0.91, with no unit, because it compares the oil's density with the density of water.
options.B: It is 0.91 g/cm³, because relative density is just another way of writing density.
options.C: It is 1.1, with no unit, because water's density must be divided by the oil's density.
options.D: It is 0.91 g, because the unit of volume cancels out when the densities are divided.

subject: science
stem: Meera measures the density of a copper vessel at home and finds it to be 8.9 g/cm³. The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. She writes in her notebook: “The relative density of copper is 8.9 g/cm³.” Which statement about her answer is correct?

options.A: It is correct, because relative density has the same unit as density.
options.B: It is wrong, because relative density has no unit; she should write 8.9.
options.C: It is wrong, because relative density should be written in kg/m³.
options.D: It is correct, because copper is denser than water.

subject: science
stem:
Falguni reads that aluminium has density 2.7 g/cm³. Relative density with respect to water equals the density of a substance divided by the density of water at that temperature, so the density units cancel and the result is a number without units.

Which claim about aluminium's relative density is correct?

options.A: It is 2.7, a number without units, because dividing by water's density cancels the density units.
options.B: It is 2.7 g/cm³, keeping the same unit as density.
options.C: It is 2.7 even if the comparison with water at that temperature is ignored.
options.D: It is 3.7, found by adding aluminium's 2.7 to water's density of about 1.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meena fills a balloon with air and ties its mouth tightly. She then places the balloon inside a freezer for some time.

The balloon shrinks slightly.

What happens to the density of the air inside the balloon?

options.A: It increases, because cooling brings the air particles closer together, reducing the volume.
options.B: It decreases, because cooling always decreases the density of a gas.
options.C: It stays the same, because the amount of air in the balloon does not change.
options.D: It becomes zero, because cooling stops the movement of air particles.

subject: science
stem:
Meera does a simple experiment at home. She fills a balloon with air and keeps a steel spoon in the kitchen. She then warms both gently in the sunlight and later presses the balloon with her hands.

Which statement about density is correct?

options.A: Heating the steel spoon spreads its particles apart, so its density decreases noticeably.
options.B: Pressing the balloon brings the air particles closer, so the density of the air inside increases.
options.C: Heating the air in the balloon increases its density because the particles move faster.
options.D: The spoon and the air change density equally because density never depends on the state of matter.

subject: science
stem:
Diya heats air in a sealed syringe; the air expands, its volume rises, and its density falls as particles spread farther apart. Density does not depend on shape or size alone, but heating, cooling, and pressure can change it. She then cools another sample of the same air and raises the pressure by pushing the plunger. Pressure mainly changes the density of gases, not of solids and liquids.

Which prediction matches how temperature and pressure change density?

options.A: Heating decreases density by spreading particles farther apart; raising pressure on a gas increases density by decreasing volume.
options.B: Heating increases density because hot air is always heavier for the same volume.
options.C: Raising pressure changes the density of solids and liquids as much as it changes the density of gases.
options.D: Density depends only on shape and size, not on temperature or pressure.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Meena drops a small steel nail and a large wooden log into a tub of water at home.

The tiny nail sinks but the heavy log floats.

What is the correct explanation?

options.A: The nail sinks because small objects are always heavier than large objects.
options.B: Steel has a greater density than water, so the nail sinks, while wood has a lower density than water, so the log floats.
options.C: The log floats because bigger objects always float, whatever material they are made of.
options.D: The nail sinks because its surface is smooth, and smooth objects always sink.

subject: science
stem:
In her kitchen, Priya drops a steel spoon and a plastic spoon of the same size into a bowl of water. The steel spoon sinks because its density is ……1…… that of water. The plastic spoon floats because its density is ……2…… that of water.

Which words correctly complete gaps 1 and 2?

options.A: 1 greater than; 2 greater than
options.B: 1 greater than; 2 less than
options.C: 1 less than; 2 greater than
options.D: 1 less than; 2 less than

subject: science
stem:
Falguni holds a wooden stick and an iron rod of the same size; the iron rod feels heavier. Density can differ even when size is the same, so an object that feels heavy may still float if its density is low. Later she sees ice floating on liquid water because ice is lighter than liquid water.

Which claim best explains floating or sinking here?

options.A: Density matters more than size alone; ice is lighter than liquid water, so the ice floats.
options.B: The iron rod feels heavier only because it is larger than the wooden stick.
options.C: Ice floats because it is heavier than liquid water.
options.D: Any object that feels heavy must sink in liquid water, even if its density is low.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera notices that the shiny steel bowl used in her kitchen reflects her face from the surface that bulges outwards. Her brother Arjun says the spoon's hollow side also acts as a mirror. Which statements correctly describe these spherical mirrors?

options.A: The bowl's outward-bulging reflecting surface is concave, and the spoon's hollow reflecting surface is convex.
options.B: The bowl's outward-bulging reflecting surface is convex, and the spoon's hollow reflecting surface is concave.
options.C: Both the bowl's bulging surface and the spoon's hollow surface are concave mirrors.
options.D: Both the bowl's bulging surface and the spoon's hollow surface are convex mirrors.

subject: science
stem:
Meera's mother uses a shiny steel ladle in the kitchen. Meera looks at the inside of the ladle's bowl, where her face appears magnified and upright when she holds it close. The inside of the bowl is the reflecting surface, and it curves inwards like the inside of a spoon.
Which type of spherical mirror does this reflecting surface behave like?

options.A: a convex mirror, because the surface bulges outwards towards her face
options.B: a concave mirror, because the reflecting surface curves inwards
options.C: a plane mirror, because the steel surface is smooth and shiny
options.D: a convex mirror, because all shiny metal objects behave as convex mirrors

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows two spherical mirrors. Shading marks the non-reflecting back of each mirror. Light comes from the object side shown.

Which statement correctly names the mirrors from the way their reflecting surfaces curve?

options.A: Mirror X is concave and Mirror Y is convex.
options.B: Mirror X is a plane mirror and Mirror Y is concave.
options.C: Both mirrors are convex because both outlines look curved.
options.D: Mirror X is convex because its back looks hollow on the shaded side.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows two spherical mirrors. Shading marks the non-reflecting back of each mirror. Light comes from the object side shown.

Bilal names each mirror from the way its reflecting surface curves.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Mirror X is concave and Mirror Y is convex.
options.B: Mirror X is a plane mirror and Mirror Y is concave.
options.C: Both mirrors are convex because both outlines look curved.
options.D: Mirror X is convex because its shaded back looks hollow.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Priya looks into three mirrors at a science exhibition in her school in Pune.
In mirror 1, her image is erect and the same size as her face.
In mirror 2, when she stands close, her image is erect and enlarged.
In mirror 3, her image is always erect and smaller than her face, no matter where she stands.
Which row correctly names the three mirrors?

options.A: mirror 1: convex, mirror 2: plane, mirror 3: concave
options.B: mirror 1: plane, mirror 2: concave, mirror 3: convex
options.C: mirror 1: concave, mirror 2: convex, mirror 3: plane
options.D: mirror 1: plane, mirror 2: convex, mirror 3: concave

subject: science
stem:
Meena stands in front of three different mirrors at a science mela in her school. In mirror 1, her image is erect and the same size as her. In mirror 2, when she stands very close, her image is erect and enlarged. In mirror 3, her image is always erect and smaller than her.
Which row correctly names the three mirrors?

options.A: Mirror 1: concave, Mirror 2: plane, Mirror 3: convex
options.B: Mirror 1: plane, Mirror 2: concave, Mirror 3: convex
options.C: Mirror 1: plane, Mirror 2: convex, Mirror 3: concave
options.D: Mirror 1: convex, Mirror 2: concave, Mirror 3: plane

subject: science
stem:
Padma stands at the same small distance in front of three mirrors. The diagram summarises the image of her face in each mirror.

Which identification is correct?

options.A: P is plane, Q is concave, R is convex.
options.B: P is convex, Q is plane, R is concave.
options.C: All three must be plane mirrors: every image is erect.
options.D: Q is convex: a larger image always means a wider view.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Qadir stands at the same small distance in front of three mirrors. The diagram summarises the image of his face in each mirror.

Which identification is correct?

options.A: P is plane, Q is concave, R is convex.
options.B: P is convex, Q is plane, R is concave.
options.C: All three must be plane mirrors because every image is erect.
options.D: Q is convex: a larger image always means a wider view.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Ritu's father fits a convex mirror as the side-view mirror on his scooter. A similar convex mirror is also fixed at a sharp turn near her school gate.
Which statement best explains why convex mirrors are chosen for these uses?

options.A: Convex mirrors show objects at their actual size, so distances are judged correctly.
options.B: Convex mirrors form erect, smaller images and give a wider field of view, so more of the surroundings can be seen.
options.C: Convex mirrors form magnified images, so small objects behind can be seen clearly.
options.D: Convex mirrors converge sunlight, so the image formed is brighter than in a plane mirror.

subject: science
stem: Meera's father has fitted a convex mirror at the gate of their apartment building in Pune so that the security guard can watch a wide stretch of the road. Why is a convex mirror used here instead of a plane mirror?

options.A: It forms an image larger than the object, so vehicles look bigger.
options.B: It forms a real, inverted image that can be seen clearly at night.
options.C: It gives an erect, smaller image and a wider field of view of the road.
options.D: It reflects sunlight better, so it needs no electricity.

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows a convex mirror fixed at a sharp bend on a road so drivers can see traffic around the corner. Plane mirrors and concave mirrors are also discussed. The glass looks shiny.

Why is a convex mirror chosen for this use?

options.A: It forms erect, smaller images and gives a wider field of view than a plane mirror.
options.B: It forms a magnified image so distant vehicles look larger than life.
options.C: Any curved mirror works the same, so a concave mirror would serve equally well here.
options.D: It is chosen only because the glass looks shiny, not because of image size or field of view.

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows three everyday uses of a convex mirror: a scooter side-view mirror, a mirror at a sharp road bend, and a shop surveillance mirror.

Why is a convex mirror chosen for these uses?

options.A: It forms erect, smaller images and gives a wider field of view than a plane mirror.
options.B: It forms a magnified image so distant objects look larger than life.
options.C: Any curved mirror works the same, so a concave mirror would serve equally well here.
options.D: It is chosen only because the glass looks shiny, not because of image size or field of view.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Priya shines a torch at a plane mirror in her classroom. The light ray strikes the mirror so that it makes an angle of 30° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection, measured from the normal?

subject: science
stem:
Priya is doing a science activity at home. She shines a torch beam onto a flat mirror fixed on her study table. The beam hits the mirror so that the ray makes an angle of 25° with the mirror surface.
Her teacher says the angle of incidence must be measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.
What is the angle of incidence?

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows a ray of light reflected from a plane mirror in Shreya's optics activity. Angles at the point of incidence are labelled P, Q, R and S.

Which pair are the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection?

options.A: Q and R
options.B: P and S
options.C: P and Q
options.D: R and S

author: grok

subject: science
stem:
Priya does a light experiment at home in Jaipur. She shines a torch beam onto a small mirror lying flat on a sheet of white cardboard and marks the reflected beam on the sheet.
Her brother bends the cardboard and says the reflected beam, the incident beam and the normal can now lie in different planes.
Which statement is correct?

options.A: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray must always lie in the same plane.
options.B: The incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane only when the sheet is flat.
options.C: The incident ray and the reflected ray lie in the same plane, but the normal may lie in a different plane.
options.D: The three lines never lie in one plane because light travels in straight lines.

subject: science
stem: Meena shines a torch onto a plane mirror fixed on the wall of her classroom. She holds a white sheet of card so that the incident ray and the normal to the mirror both lie along the sheet. What must be true for the reflected ray to appear on the same sheet?

options.A: The reflected ray always lies in the same plane as the incident ray and the normal, so it will appear on the sheet
options.B: The reflected ray lies in a different plane from the incident ray, so it cannot appear on the sheet
options.C: The reflected ray lies in the same plane as the incident ray but not the normal, so it may not appear on the sheet
options.D: The reflected ray can lie in any plane, so bending the sheet makes no difference to where it appears

subject: science
stem:
Diya shines a torch at a plane mirror, as in the diagram. The dashed line is drawn at 90° to the mirror.

Which statement about the incident ray, that dashed line, and the reflected ray is correct?

options.A: The dashed line is just another name for the incident ray, so only two lines matter.
options.B: The incident ray, the dashed normal, and the reflected ray all lie in one plane.
options.C: The three lines need not share a plane; only the hatch marks along the mirror matter.
options.D: The same-plane rule is only for curved mirrors, not for a plane mirror.

author: grok

subject: science
stem: Meera shines a torch so that several parallel light rays fall on three different mirrors in her science lab at school: a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror. Which row correctly describes how the parallel rays are reflected by all three mirrors?

options.A: All three mirrors reflect the parallel rays as parallel rays, because each ray obeys the law of reflection.
options.B: The plane mirror keeps the rays parallel, the concave mirror makes them converge, and the convex mirror makes them diverge.
options.C: The plane mirror keeps the rays parallel, the concave mirror makes them diverge, and the convex mirror makes them converge.
options.D: The plane mirror makes the rays converge, the concave mirror keeps them parallel, and the convex mirror makes them diverge.

subject: science
stem:
Priya shines three narrow, parallel beams of light at a convex mirror fitted on the gate of her house.
How will the beams travel after reflection from the mirror?

options.A: They remain parallel to each other.
options.B: They converge to a point in front of the mirror.
options.C: They diverge as if coming from a point behind the mirror.
options.D: They are absorbed by the mirror surface.

subject: science
stem:
Imran sends several torch rays that are parallel to one another onto the plane mirror shown below.

What happens to those rays after reflection?

options.A: They meet at a point behind the mirror.
options.B: They stay parallel to one another after reflection from the flat sheet.
options.C: They spread apart as if the sheet were a convex surface.
options.D: Only the hatch marks on the back of the mirror decide whether the rays meet.

subject: science
stem:
Meera places a concave mirror facing the Sun outside her home in Jaipur. The reflected sunlight forms a small bright spot on a piece of paper, and the paper starts to smoke.
Why does the concave mirror make the paper hot enough to smoke?

options.A: The mirror absorbs the sunlight and becomes hot, and the paper touching the mirror's surface gets heated.
options.B: The mirror spreads the sunlight evenly over the paper, so the whole sheet slowly warms up.
options.C: The mirror is curved inward, so it converges the reflected sunlight into a small spot where concentrated energy raises the temperature.
options.D: The mirror reflects light without any focusing, but paper always catches fire when sunlight falls on it.

subject: science
stem:
Meera uses a concave shaving mirror to focus sunlight onto a dry scrap of newspaper in her courtyard. After a few moments, the paper begins to smoke at one small bright spot.
Why does the paper start to burn at that spot?

options.A: The mirror makes the sunlight warm as soon as the light touches the mirror's surface, and this heat passes to the paper.
options.B: The concave mirror reflects the parallel rays of sunlight so that they meet at one small point, concentrating the light energy there and raising the temperature enough to ignite the paper.
options.C: The mirror spreads the sunlight evenly over the paper, so the whole sheet warms up slowly until it catches fire.
options.D: The shiny surface of the mirror produces its own heat, which is transferred to the newspaper placed near it.

subject: science
stem:
The diagram shows sunlight reaching a concave mirror. Parallel rays meet at one place on a scrap of paper.

Why does a bright hot spot form on the paper?

options.A: The concave mirror reflects the parallel rays so that they meet at one small point, concentrating the light energy there.
options.B: The concave mirror spreads the parallel rays evenly across the paper, so the whole paper warms at once.
options.C: Any mirror makes a hot spot on the paper; the concave shape does not matter.
options.D: The paper heats first, and that heat then bends the rays toward the bright spot.

options.B: an object that is thicker in the middle than at the edges
options.C: an object that has the same thickness all over

options.B: Through P, Q, and R the letter looks erect and enlarged.

options.B: Find the time from the shortest shadow on day 1 to the shortest shadow on day 2.

options.B: A day is set by the Sun's apparent daily cycle, a lunar month by the Moon's full phase cycle, and a year by Earth's journey around the Sun.
options.C: A day, a month, and a year are only calendar words and are not linked to any sky cycle.

options.A: A day follows the Moon's phases; a lunar month follows the Sun's daily path; a year follows the stars alone.
options.B: A day follows the Sun's apparent daily cycle; a lunar month follows the Moon's phase cycle; a year follows Earth's journey around the Sun.

options.B: The seasons are caused by clouds and rainfall

subject: science
chapter_label: The night sky: Moon and calendars
stem: Meera's grandmother follows a purely lunar calendar in which each month begins with a new Moon, and 12 such lunar months make one lunar year of about 354 days. Meera notices that a festival fixed to a particular lunar month falls in winter one year but, after several years, falls in the rainy season. Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.A: The Moon's phases change randomly, so no calendar based on them can ever repeat in a regular way.
options.B: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar year ends earlier and the months drift through the seasons.
options.C: The seasons themselves become a little shorter each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
options.D: The Moon takes exactly 30 days to complete its phases, which matches the seasonal year, so any mismatch must be due to counting errors.

stem:

Why does a purely lunar calendar not keep the same months aligned with the same seasons year after year?

options.A: The Moon's phases change randomly, so no lunar calendar can repeat in a regular way.
options.B: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, which is shorter than the roughly 365-day seasonal year, so the lunar year ends earlier and the months drift through the seasons.
options.C: The seasons themselves become a little shorter each year, so the lunar months can no longer keep pace with them.
options.D: Twelve lunar months total more than 365 days, so the lunar year runs long and the months drift the other way.

options.C: The extra day is added only as a festival holiday and has no scientific reason.
